## Editing a live agent's config CANNOT reach an in-flight orchestration — it carries its own snapshot

- **footprint:** `agent_definitions.default_config` · `orchestration_states.workflow_plan` ·
  any migration under `docs/agent_docs/sql_for_agents/` that edits a live agent's
  workflow, prompt_template or step config
- **fires when:** you are about to change a live agent's config and stop to ask
  "is it safe while a run is in flight?" — or, the mirror image, when you edit a
  prompt *because* a run is going wrong and expect it to take effect
- **the tell:** **there is no tell in either direction, and the two errors are
  opposite.** Guessing "unsafe" costs you a quiet window that on a tree this
  many sessions share may never arrive — I nearly held a migration indefinitely
  behind two concurrently-running councils. Guessing "safe to hot-fix" is worse:
  the run finishes on the OLD text and the verdict looks like your fix did
  nothing, so you go hunting for a second bug that does not exist
- **the check:** ask the running orchestration what it is holding —
  ```sql
  SELECT orchestration_id,
         (workflow_plan->'steps'-><step>->'config' ? 'prompt_template') AS carries_own_copy,
         length(workflow_plan->'steps'-><step>->'config'->>'prompt_template')
  FROM orchestration_states WHERE status NOT IN ('COMPLETED','FAILED','CANCELLED');
  ```
  Measured 2026-08-10 on two live council runs: both carried a full copy of every
  seat template (4,530 chars for `review_mission`, matching the then-current row
  exactly). **An orchestration executes from that captured plan.** So: config
  edits are safe to apply at any time, AND they only affect orchestrations
  created afterwards. Confirm empirically after the edit — calls logged *after*
  migration 377 landed still began with the OLD prompt ordering, which is the
  positive confirmation, not an anomaly
- **the corollary that bites hardest:** "I fixed the prompt, why is it still
  behaving the old way" during an active incident. It is not a caching problem
  and not a stale pod — that run was committed to the old text the moment it
  started. Cancel and re-dispatch, or wait it out
- **source:** hit directly, `council_gate_cost` lane 2026-08-10 while applying
  migration 377 (17 council seat templates) with two councils mid-chain. The
  migration's original banner said "do not apply while a run is in flight"; that
  was a guess, it was wrong, and the corrected banner now carries the query
- **added:** 2026-08-10, council_gate_cost lane

### `computed_values` reads a `display:none` subtree perfectly well — so it pins the ARITHMETIC and says nothing about whether the visitor could SEE it

- **footprint:** `internal/adapters/browserrunner/run_checks_action.go` (`runComputedValues`, `chromiumPage.Text` :1288 `InnerText()`) · `doc_plans` ```criteria fences using `computed_values` · `toolgolden.py --emit-criteria` · any reveal-style tool (results panel that starts hidden and is shown on submit)
- **fires when:** you author a `computed_values` fence for a calculator whose results panel starts hidden, and reason that because `Text()` is `InnerText()`, a hidden element reads `""` — therefore the value check *already* proves the reveal happened and a separate visibility check would be redundant. That reasoning is wrong, and it is the natural reasoning: `InnerText` really is render-aware for some things (it applies `text-transform`, see below), which makes "and therefore it is empty when hidden" feel like the same fact.
- **the tell:** none, because the fence goes green either way and the omission only shows up as a check you never wrote. The HTML spec has `innerText` fall back to `textContent` when the element **is not being rendered**, so a `display:none` subtree returns its full text. A tool that computes every figure correctly and then never shows the visitor anything passes a `computed_values`-only fence.
- **measured, twice, and it could have come out otherwise** (2026-08-10, robot-hands `tool-grip-force-friction-calculator`): (1) a mutant replacing `resultsPanel.classList.add('visible')` with a class that matches no rule left the panel `display:none` — all five computed values still matched, and the two other reveal-dependent checks passed too; (2) an isolating probe that changed **only CSS** (`.results-panel.visible { display: block }` → `display: none`), touching no JS, also passed. Had the premise held, both would have gone red.
- **the check:** carry the visibility claim in its **own** check — `interaction` with `expect.selector` naming the revealed state (`#resultsPanel.visible`, or `#x:not(.hidden)`) — and prove it separately with a mutant that breaks only the reveal. Do not let `computed_values` stand in for it. And when you write the mutants file, do **not** list the value checks in that mutant's `expect_fail`: they will not fail, and a mutant whose claimed blast radius is wrong is caught by the prover as a MISS, which is the good case, but only if you re-run it.
- **the sibling trap, same run:** `computed_values` compares **rendered** text, so a golden copied from the JS source string is wrong for any element carrying `text-transform`. MatchMatrix builds `'Match'` / `'No match'` and the badge carries `text-transform: uppercase`, so the fence must assert `MATCH` / `NO MATCH`. This is the right way round — it pins what the visitor sees — but it costs one red trial if you derive the golden from the source alone. Derive from the JS, then **corroborate against the live tool** before persisting.
- **source:** 2026-08-10, staged_component_build lane, batch 8 (`tool-grip-force-friction-calculator`, `tool-matchmatrix`). The false premise was written down the same day in this lane's own NOTES and in `manifest_batch8.json`'s `tool-setup-builder` contract ("`InnerText()`, which reads `""` on a hidden element") — that PLAN's fence is sound anyway, because its `.db-value` spans ship EMPTY in the served HTML, so the check discriminates static from driven for a different and genuine reason. The stated reason is what is wrong, not the fence.
- **added:** 2026-08-10, staged_component_build lane (batch 8)

### On this estate the AGENT UNDER TEST usually has not run — four verifications in one lane, three unobservable for want of demand

- **footprint:** `orchestration_states`, `owner_agent_type`, `agent_error_log`, `verify-later`, acceptance evidence, `vet-practice-verifier`, `content-reviewer`, `diagnose_council_decide`, post-roll verification
- **fires when:** you write a `verify-later`, an acceptance section, or a "did the fix work?" query for anything that runs on a schedule, a trigger, or a lane nobody is currently driving. No symptom needed — the check runs clean and returns a number.
- **the trap:** the fleet is large and busy, so "the platform is clearly alive" feels like it licenses reading a zero as success. It does not, because **traffic is fleet-wide and demand is per-path**, and most individual agents are idle most of the time. Measured over one lane's four verifications on 2026-08-09/10: the three residual `agent_error_log` producers filed **0** rows post-roll *and had stopped four days before the roll*; `vet-practice-verifier` had **0** runs in the retained window, so the only step configured to exercise a new resolver never executed; `content-reviewer` had **0** runs, so a predicted config-key warning had no opportunity to fire. **Three of four verifications were unobservable, and every one of them returned a clean, quotable number.**
- **why the wrong result looks exactly like the right one:** the expected outcome of a successful fix *is* a low or zero number, so the result you get is the result you wanted. The fleet-wide control that is supposed to protect you (`count(*)` over the window, `count(DISTINCT agent_type)`) **passes honestly** — it proves the pipeline, and the pipeline is genuinely fine. Nothing in either output mentions the agent you actually changed.
- **the check, before writing OR reading any verify-later:**
  ```sql
  -- did the thing under test run at all, in the window you are about to quote?
  SELECT count(*) FROM orchestration_states WHERE owner_agent_type = '<the agent>';
  SELECT count(*) FROM agent_error_log     WHERE action = '<the producer>' AND occurred_at > '<boundary>';
  -- and for a baseline, read its TAIL rather than its total: a producer that went
  -- quiet BEFORE your change shipped makes the comparison unfalsifiable
  SELECT occurred_at::date, count(*) FROM agent_error_log
  WHERE action IN (<producers>) AND occurred_at > now() - interval '14 days' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
  ```
  Zero demand ⇒ the honest verdict is **UNOBSERVABLE**, never *passing*. ⚠ `orchestration_states` retains ~24h, so "0 runs" there means "not in the last day" — a longer-lived question needs a different witness.
- **what to do instead, since waiting is usually not a plan:** **induce the condition**, and say in the `verify-later` that you did. The worked example is `platform/orchestration/resumed_step_provenance_test.go` — the live case it covers had not occurred fleet-wide since 2026-07-26, so it was reproduced in a harness that builds the state the way production builds it (round-tripping real headers) rather than hand-assembling a convenient version. A `verify-later` that can only be discharged by an event nobody controls is a `verify-never`; write it as an induced check from the start.
- **source:** 2026-08-09/10, `rfc012_await_findings` lane, chassis `v1.0.1277`→`v1.0.1283`. `RFC_019` §12, `WRONG_CALLS.md` 2026-08-10, `WFA-012`'s and `RSH-009`'s verify-later lines (both now carry the demand caveat inline).
- **verification:** settled first-hand — every count above was run against the live DB on 2026-08-10 and is quoted in the cited entries.
- **added:** 2026-08-10, rfc012_await_findings lane

### `strings` is NOT INSTALLED in the fleet's debian-slim image, so the standard pod-grep verification returns a SILENT 0 there — "I could not look" wearing the exact costume of "your fix is not live"

- **footprint:** `build/docker/backend/browser-runner-adapter.dockerfile` (`FROM debian:bookworm-slim`) · CLAUDE.md § "Building & deploying images" (the `strings /app/<svc> | grep -c` recipe) · any `kubectl exec … strings … 2>/dev/null` · `makefile` `verify-agent-images`
- **fires when:** you verify *any* deploy the way this estate tells you to — `kubectl exec <pod> -- sh -c 'strings /app/<svc> | grep -c "<marker>"'`. Thirteen of the fourteen backend services are alpine and `strings` works. **`browser-runner-adapter` is debian-slim** (Chromium needs glibc, stated in its dockerfile) and ships **no binutils**, so `strings` is command-not-found there.
- **the tell:** none, and the `2>/dev/null` that every published recipe carries is what destroys it. `strings` writes its "not found" to stderr, which is discarded; the empty pipe reaches `grep -c`, which prints **`0`**. You get a clean, confident zero. **Measured 2026-08-10:** a correctly-stamped `browser-runner-adapter` read as unstamped, and I briefly believed a brand-new provenance mechanism had caught a stale image on its first run. It had not — the check had.
- **the check:** never use `strings` in a container probe. `grep -a` reads the binary directly and needs nothing installed, and **`/proc/1/exe` resolves the RUNNING binary** regardless of image base *or* binary path — which also retires the per-service path guessing (`/app/x` on most, `/root/x` on `git-adapter`, `/x` on `remote-job-spawner`; and `ls` on those can fail on *permissions*, giving a second false "not there"). Verify a KNOWN value: `kubectl -n ai-persona-system exec <pod> -- grep -aq "<expected-sha-or-marker>" /proc/1/exe && echo MATCH || echo "NO MATCH"`. **Before believing any negative, run the same probe against a string that MUST be present** — the positive control is the only thing that separates "absent" from "I could not look".
- **the trap INSIDE the fix, which cost a second wrong answer:** dropping `strings` for `grep -aoE "[0-9a-f]{40}"` to *discover* the sha also drops `strings`' **line boundaries**, so `^`/`$` become meaningless and the match lands inside Go's internal digit table — every service returns `0001020304050607080910111213141516171819`, identically and with total confidence. **A discovery grep over an unanchored byte stream cannot be trusted; only a verification grep for a value you already know can.** Ask "does this pod carry sha X", never "what sha does this pod carry".
- **source:** `bugs_open/153` lane, verifying BLD-019 on the v1.0.1283 roll; both traps measured on live pods, both directions, on alpine and debian-slim. Fix in `makefile` `verify-agent-images` (commit `c4a932680`).
- **added:** 2026-08-10, bugfix_153_build_provenance lane

### `spec->>'audit_source'` is the ONLY thing that names a work item's producer — `item_type` hides the split and `created_by` bottoms out at `generic`

- **footprint:** `site_work_items.item_type`, `site_work_items.spec`, `created_by`, `discovery_checks/verifiers.go` (`RegisterVerifier` / `GetVerifier`), `complete_work_item_verification.go`, `write_audit_findings_action.go` (`designItemTypes` / `designRouting`)
- **fires when:** you register a verifier for an `item_type`; you route a new producer onto an existing `item_type`; you census "who files this type" or "how is this type doing"; you read a `complete` row as evidence that something was repaired.
- **the tell:** there is none at completion time, and that is the whole trap. When two producers share an `item_type` and only one wrote the verifier, the verifier grades the other's items against a predicate about a different defect — and because it is **correct for its own question**, it returns `Resolved:true` and the item closes clean. Nothing errors, nothing is mis-written, no log line is anomalous. Measured on the one live instance (`bugs_open/213`): 11 of 11 design-audit items closed `complete` and **not one has ever reached `unresolved` or `detected`**, while all 8 items that ever failed to close belonged to the producer who wrote the verifier. The worked case closed in 3m17s against a component last touched **10.5 hours before the item existed**, and the page still measures 1.72:1.
- **the check:** never ask this question with `GROUP BY item_type` — it shows one population and hides the split. Group by the producer: `count(*) FILTER (WHERE spec->>'audit_source' = '<producer>')`. **Do not reach for `created_by`** — it is `config[source]` falling back to `params.AgentType`, bottoming out at the literal `generic`, which carries 20+ item_types. Before registering a verifier, run the fleet check: `SELECT item_type, count(DISTINCT COALESCE(spec->>'audit_source','<none>')) FROM site_work_items WHERE item_type IN (<the RegisterVerifier list>) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC;` — a `2` there means your verifier is already grading somebody else's items. The predicate is disconfirmable: it returns 2 where the shape exists and 1 elsewhere. **And do not grade a suspected instance by re-running the verifier** — it will pass again, for the same correct reason; grade the item against its own `spec.acceptance_test`, or at the served artefact.
- **the second trap inside the first:** a `complete` COUNT is not a false-complete count. Of the 11 above, one is confirmed false at the served artefact and one measures CLEAN in an independent baseline. Quoting the count as damage overstates it in exactly the direction nobody audits.
- **relations:** `bugs_open/213` (mechanism, census, the refuted producer-list candidate), WII-013 (the `VerifierPolicy.Grades` remit contract that closes it, and the producer sets), WII-011 / RFC_017 (a *different* hole in the same registry — that one needs an error to fire, this one needs nothing), `bugs_closed/077` (detector predicate wider than its handler's remit — the same shape one level down).

### An ownership check that reads COMMITS cannot see the session that is fixing it right now

- **footprint:** `scripts/who-owns.py`, `git log`, the session-start `git status` snapshot, `bugs_open/`
- **fires when:** you pick up a bug, route work at an existing bug, or conclude a lane is dormant — i.e. every time you decide what to work on.
- **the tell:** none, and the checks *agree with each other*, which reads as corroboration. `who-owns.py` reports commits; `git log` over the bug's code paths reports commits; "no workstream directory exists" is a commit-derived fact too; and the session-start `git status` block is a **snapshot** that CLAUDE.md itself says goes stale within minutes. Four checks, one blindness. On 2026-08-10 all four said `bugs_open/214` was unowned while another session had 116 uncommitted lines and three untracked files in its exact code paths — ~1 hour of investigation spent before a comment dated *today*, in a file with no commit from today, gave it away by accident.
- **the check:** run `git status --short <the code paths the bug file names in its own §Cause>` **FIRST**, before reading the bug, and re-run it rather than trusting the session-start snapshot. `git status --short | grep -E '\.go$'` shows every session's in-flight Go work in one line. **An untracked new file sitting next to a bug's cited paths is the strongest ownership signal there is** — stronger than any commit, because it means someone is mid-fix. Then, and only then, spend `who-owns.py` on the commit history.
- **relations:** `WRONG_CALLS.md` 2026-08-10 (the full incident and its cost), the memory entry `who-owns-is-blind-to-uncommitted-sessions`, `a-pathspec-commit-still-takes-a-same-file-passenger` (the mirror-image hazard: your own edits leaving in someone else's commit — which also happened in the same session, to `verifier_coverage_test.go`, swept into `d644723b8`).

### One `make release` is NOT one source revision — each of the 14 builds resolves `HEAD` separately, so a release straddles whatever other sessions commit during it

- **footprint:** `makefile` (`REF ?= HEAD` at :111, `git rev-parse` inside `ref_build` at :128, `release` at :2357), `make release`, `make build-*`, `org.opencontainers.image.revision`, `pkg/buildinfo.GitCommit`
- **fires when:** you run or read a release; you say "the fleet is on v1.0.NNNN"; you use one service's build stamp to conclude a commit did or did not ship fleet-wide; you plan a change whose halves live in different services (a shared helper plus its callers, a producer plus its consumer).
- **the tell:** none whatsoever, and every instrument agrees with every other. The tag is identical on all 14 deployments, `kubectl get pods` is uniform, the roll is green, and each service's own `build provenance` line is *correct for that service*. The disagreement is only visible if you compare the stamps **across** services, which nothing does automatically. **Measured 2026-08-11:** `v1.0.1284` shipped `55fc8fc35` on five services, `e2afedaaf` on one, `a41dec8e5` on eight — a 6m22s build with two other sessions' commits landing inside it. That instance was harmless (docs + two `_test.go`); the same six minutes containing a platform commit ships half a fleet with it and half without, under one version number.
- **the check:** compare the labels, not the tag — `for S in <the 14>; do docker image inspect docker.io/aqls/$S:$IMAGE_TAG --format '{{index .Config.Labels "org.opencontainers.image.revision"}}'; done | sort -u` must return **exactly one line**. At the cluster, the cheap per-service witness is `kubectl -n ai-persona-system logs -l app=<service> --tail=300 | grep -m1 'build provenance'` — no exec, no binary path, nothing to install, and it is the service's own statement rather than your inference from its bytes. **To prevent rather than detect:** `make release REF=$(git rev-parse HEAD) …` pins one revision for the whole sweep, works today, and needs no code change.
- **the second trap, inside the check:** `verify-agent-images` looks at **`agent-chassis` only**, and defaults `EXPECT_SHA` to live `git rev-parse HEAD` — on this tree HEAD moves within minutes of any roll, so it prints `NO MATCH` routinely and *correctly*, which trains the reader to ignore the one stanza that would catch a real problem. Read it against the **image label**, not against HEAD.
- **relations:** `bugs_open/249` (the bug, with the full build/commit timeline and ranked fixes), `bugs_open/153` + BLD-019 (the provenance stamp that made this visible — the question could not be asked before 2026-08-10), `bugs_open/237` (a service in no release path at all — adjacent failure of the same assumption that "the release covers the fleet").
- **added:** 2026-08-11, bugfix_153_build_provenance lane

### `save_page_sections` REPLACES a page's `content_data` and `rerender_page_sections` MERGES it — so a key can survive re-renders for months and die on the first real regeneration

- **footprint:** `platform/orchestration/actions/save_page_sections_action.go` (the DELETE + INSERT pair), `platform/orchestration/actions/rerender_page_sections_action.go` (`stored ⊕ fresh resolved_data`), `platform/orchestration/actions/plan_sections_action.go` (`planSection`, `handleMissingField`, `carryStored`), `page_components.content_data`, `content_components.input_schema` fields whose `source` is not `llm`
- **fires when:** you reason about whether a rebuild can lose stored content; you read either write path on its own; you change `on_missing` handling; you add a component field sourced from `site_assets.*` / `site_specs.*` / `pages.*`; or you conclude from a page's long stable history that its data is safe.
- **the tell:** none for months at a time, and the history actively lies to you. On finetuning.uk the five card image URLs were byte-identical in `page_component_history` from 2026-05-01 to 2026-08-03 across many successful rebuilds — because every one of those runs was a **re-render**, which merges. The first true content regeneration (a `tone_shift`) dropped **all 11** non-llm keys at once. The page then served five `<img src="">` *and* — worse, because it is invisible — five card links and a section CTA that vanished entirely, since those fields sit behind `{{if}}` guards. Every work item reported `complete`. **A gated field fails more quietly than an ungated one**, which is the opposite of the intuition that gating is the safe pattern.
- **why the keys go:** they are not the LLM's to emit. `plan_sections` splits schema fields by `source` and puts only `source:"llm"` in the writer's field list (the prompt says "exactly the keys listed"). A non-llm field is resolved by `sourceResolver`; if that resolves nothing, `on_missing` — which **defaults to `skip_field` when the schema omits it** — omits the key with an Info log, *even when the field is `required:true`*. `missingRequiredLLMFields`, the render gate that would refuse an empty section, exempts it in one line: `if source != "llm" || !required { continue }`.
- **the check:** ask which *kind* of run you are looking at before believing a page's stable history — `spec->>'reason'` on the work item (`section_data_resolved`/`image_landed` = the merging re-render; a content item like `tone_shift`/`content_rewrite` = the replacing regeneration). To see whether a component is exposed at all, list its non-llm fields and compare against a live row, remembering the fields are nested one level down: `SELECT f.key, f.value->>'source' FROM content_components cc, LATERAL jsonb_each(COALESCE(cc.input_schema->'fields', cc.input_schema->'properties')) f WHERE cc.id='<id>' AND COALESCE(f.value->>'source','llm') <> 'llm';` A `jsonb_each(input_schema)` without that COALESCE returns the wrapper keys and reads as "no fields".
- **since 2026-08-11 (PBP-039) the build path carries these keys forward from the page's own deployed row — and that carry is now the ONLY thing making it lossless.** Reading `save_page_sections` alone still shows an unconditional replace, and on a healthy site it looks harmless because the carry silently filled the gap upstream. Do not remove it, do not reorder it ahead of the alias chains (that would prefer a stale stored value over a corrected live source), and do not assume the re-render merge covers the build path: it never did.
- **the CHEAP check, added 2026-08-12 after this bit again — one query, no new tool, and it is the only one of six that saw the damage.** Before and after ANY regeneration, count the anchors per component and diff the pair:
  `SELECT p.name, pc.slot_name, (SELECT count(*) FROM regexp_matches(pc.rendered_html,'href="','g')) AS links FROM page_components pc JOIN pages p ON p.id=pc.page_id WHERE p.site_id='<site>' ORDER BY p.name, pc.position;`
  On webdesign.uk that afternoon, a `content_rewrite` deleted **14 anchors across 7 components** — every CTA button on four pages — while the claims scan returned 0 findings, the bodies GREW, the retired-term greps were clean and the served pages carried the new copy. **Five checks green, and not one could see a missing `href`**, because each was aimed at what the change was FOR (banned phrases, truncation, the terms named, arrival at the box) and none at what it might COST. A link-set gate was running and passed — armed on the ONE page judged risky, while the damage landed on the four it was not pointed at: **a gate covers what you point it at, and its green light will feel like more than it is.** Generalise it: for a regeneration, diff the INVARIANTS (link count, image count, component count) and treat whatever you did not intend to change as the finding. Full account: `WRONG_CALLS.md` 2026-08-12.
- ~~**and the carry does NOT cover `source: "renderer"` fields**~~ — **RETRACTED 2026-08-12, hours after it was written: the `090` (`97ef39f0-19df-4935-834d-c80514fbc43e`) returned REFUTED.** The reading was that `sourceResolver.resolve` short-circuits `source: "renderer"` to `(nil, TRUE)`, so the field is never *missing* and `carryStored` never runs. **Do not build on it.** The run is not decisive either, for a reason worth more than the hypothesis was: the filing session **repaired `content_data` at 17:23 and started the run at 17:39**, so the verdict's citations are the restored values and it measured a repaired system. **Fix first, ask second, and the answer is about the fix** — where a repair cannot wait, point the run at `page_component_history` and say in the symptom that the live table was repaired, and when. What the run DID establish: **`bugs_open/238` as tracked in the codebase is the dead-URL-CONTROL defect** (a section that RENDERS while leaving a URL attribute empty, recorded non-fatally on the rerender path), not a `content_data` key-loss case — its own comment says so, and `next_scope` is `dead_url_guard.go` / `emitSectionDeadControlItem` / `recordDeadURLControls`. The CTA loss above is REAL and MEASURED; its cause is OPEN. Separately still true: 238's §8 banner is stale about the carry being unrolled (`agent-chassis v1.0.1291` ← `da5a7eb8f`, merge-base verified with controls both ways).
- **relations:** `bugs_open/238` (the incident, the 58→47 key diff, the fleet census of 5 damaged rows across 4 sites; and §9, the 2026-08-12 case the carry did not cover), PBP-039 (the carry) and PBP-014 (why resolved values live inside `content_data` at all), RFC_009 (why the render-time `on_missing` gate was NOT taken — ~90% of fields declare no `on_missing`), `bugs_open/178` (the standing stop sign against adding a sixth refusing floor to `save_page_sections`), STY-049 (`missingkey=zero`, the root silence), `bugs_open/236` (the same family one layer earlier, root cause unestablished), `bugs_open/229` (what a hand-patched `rendered_html` re-arms, which is how the 08-12 repair had to be made).
- **added:** 2026-08-11, bugfix_238_regeneration_key_loss lane · **extended 2026-08-12, ai_site_selling_automation lane** (the href-diff check and the renderer-source gap)

### `page_component_history` is not shaped the way its name implies — its `component_id` is the page_components ROW, and two constraints will abort your transaction

- **footprint:** `page_component_history` (`component_id`, `op`, `page_component_id` which does NOT exist), any hand-written archive/restore SQL, `save_page_sections_action.go`'s pre-DELETE snapshot
- **fires when:** you write a manual snapshot before repairing a row, or try to read a page's content history by joining the obvious way.
- **the tell:** three separate failures, each of which stops the transaction — so the danger is not silent damage but wasted cycles and, if you are running inside a bigger script, a half-applied repair if you did not wrap it in `BEGIN`. (1) There is **no `page_component_id` column**; the join key is `page_id` + `component_id`. (2) `component_id` is a **FK to `page_components(id)` — the row** — not to `content_components(id)`, even though `page_components.component_id` means exactly that; inserting the content-component id fails the FK. (3) `op` is constrained to `'overwrite' | 'delete' | NULL`; the natural `'UPDATE'` fails `pch_op_check`.
- **the second trap:** the FK is `ON DELETE SET NULL`, and `save_page_sections` archives a row then DELETEs it — so **every historic row reads `component_id IS NULL`**, which makes the column look unused and tempts you to leave it out or fill it with the wrong id. It also means you cannot select a slot's history by component id; filter on a key the payload itself carries (`h.content_data ? '<a field only this component has>'`) or on `slot_name`, which older rows also leave empty.
- **the check:** read the constraints, not just the columns — `\d page_component_history` **piped through `head` truncates exactly the block you need** (the check constraints print last). Use `SELECT conname, pg_get_constraintdef(oid) FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid='page_component_history'::regclass;` and confirm `op`'s allowed values before writing the INSERT.
- **relations:** `bugs_open/229` / STY-056 (the archive trigger and the `rendered_html` arm added to this table), `bugs_open/238` (the repair that hit all three), the existing entry noting `page_component_history.source` is a write-MODE label and not a writer.
- **added:** 2026-08-11, bugfix_238_regeneration_key_loss lane

### `code_symbols` stores Go METHODS receiver-qualified — a bare-name lookup returns 0 rows, no error, and the loop's cite-or-abstain acts on that absence
- **footprint:** `code_symbols` (`symbol`, `kind='method'`), `platform/orchestration/actions/diagnose_code_lookup_action.go` (`answerCodeCheck`, `parseSymbolQuery`, `symbolClauseFor`), `diagnose_load_runtime` code tier, any `code_request` naming a Go method, any `SELECT … FROM code_symbols WHERE symbol = '<name>'`
- **fires when:** you look up a Go **method** in the code index — by hand, or as a `code_request`/`next_scope` entry — using the name as it is written at the call site. Methods are stored under their **receiver-qualified** name: `applyResponseToState` is indexed as `(*SagaCoordinator).applyResponseToState`, and `kind` is `method`, not `func`. Plain functions in the SAME FILE are stored bare, so the two conventions sit side by side and neither is signposted
- **the tell: there is none.** An exact-match `WHERE symbol IN ('applyResponseToState')` returns **zero rows and no error**, which is indistinguishable from "this function is not indexed" and from "this function does not exist". It is worse than a plain miss in this estate because the diagnosis verdict prompt's **cite-or-abstain rule acts on absence** — so a bare-name `code_request` for a method makes the loop reason as though the code is not there. 2026-08-11 I nearly filed "the merge function at the heart of bugs_open/236 is missing from the index" on exactly this zero; the body was present all along, 4,746 chars
- **the check:** never probe the index with `=` on a name you have not confirmed the storage form of. Use `ILIKE` and let it show you the shape — `SELECT symbol, kind, path FROM code_symbols WHERE symbol ILIKE '%applyResponseToState%';` — which returns the qualified name immediately. **The free sanity check that settles it in one line:** compare the index's count for the file against the source's, `SELECT count(*) FROM code_symbols WHERE path='<file>';` versus `grep -c '^func ' <file>`. For `coordinator.go` on 2026-08-11 that was **92 vs 91** — nothing was missing at all, and any "it is absent" theory was dead before it was written
- **the inverse, for whoever writes a `code_request`:** asking for a method by its bare name is not a narrower query, it is an **unanswerable** one. Name it `(*Receiver).Method`, or use a substring query, or you will be told nothing exists and be given no reason to doubt it
- > **⚠ CORRECTED 2026-08-12 (`bugs_open/261`) — the bullet directly above is right for a `code_request` and was WRONG for a `next_scope` entry, and following it was how the defect got found.** The two paths do not share a resolver. A `code_request` queries `code_symbols`, where `(*Receiver).Method` is the only spelling that matches. A `next_scope` entry goes to `analysis.ReadSymbolBody`, whose `spanOf` split on the last dot and compared the raw `(*SagaCoordinator)` against `receiverType()`'s `SagaCoordinator` — so **the receiver-qualified form was the one spelling it could NOT resolve**, and you got `_(body unavailable — a TOOLING failure)_` with the body sitting in the index all along. Measured over all 460 bundles ever assembled: **335 lost bodies across 47 diagnosis runs, 312 of them this exact shape** (and the count grew by 14 in the forty minutes it took to write this up). **Fixed in `6911c2da4`** — `splitReceiver` now normalises `(*T).M`, `(T).M`, `*T.M` and `T.M` alike, and `spanOf` searches `FileInfo.Values` so package-level `var`/`const` resolve at all. **Go, therefore INERT until rolled: until the next fleet roll, prefer the BARE name in a `next_scope` entry and the QUALIFIED name in a `code_request`.** After the roll both spellings work everywhere and this distinction dies — verify with `git merge-base --is-ancestor 6911c2da4 <the running build's stamp>` rather than assuming.
- **source:** `diagnosis_schema_visibility` lane, 2026-08-11, verifying commission item 5 — checking the OTHER harness blocker on the `074beb8a` run before spending credits on a re-run
- **added:** 2026-08-11, diagnosis_schema_visibility lane

### A tool component that writes `color: var(--color-surface)` on `background: var(--color-primary)` is legible on 6 of 8 sites and INVISIBLE on the rest — and every selector check passes it

- **footprint:** `content_components.html_template` containing both `background: var(--color-primary)` and `color: var(--color-surface)`; `--color-surface` / `--color-primary` in any site's `/assets/css/styles.css`; `tool-setup-builder`, `tool-automation-savings-estimator`, `tool-bridging-compound`, `tool-cma-obligation-checker`, `tool-fuel-cost-estimator`, `tool-idea-stage-identifier`, `tool-rate-scenarios`; any Tier-4 fence asserting an option/CTA is present
- **fires when:** you author a fence for a tool with selectable options, you reuse an existing tool template on a new site, you read a green acceptance verdict as "the page is fine", or you conclude from a `computed_values`/`interaction` pass that a control is usable.
- **the tell: there is none in any check we run.** The token pair means "paint the selected state in the brand colour and write on it in the page-background colour" — which silently assumes `--color-surface` is a PALE shade. It is a variable; on a dark-themed site it is dark too. `dartsonline.com` resolves `--color-primary #1A1F2E` and `--color-surface #1E2436`: **contrast 1.06 : 1**, against a WCAG AA floor of 4.5. The correct pairing on the same page (`--color-text` on primary) is 14.65 : 1. The tool's 15 checks all passed in the same run, because presence, computation, reveal and console-cleanliness are every one of them true — **the text is there, it is styled, it is simply the same colour as what is behind it.** Note also there is usually no `label` BASE colour rule, only `input:checked + label`, so exactly one option per group is hit — the default-checked one — which reads as a content quirk rather than a systematic fault.
- **the check:** never infer contrast from the source — the literal `var(--x)` in the template tells you nothing about what it resolves to. Fetch the site's own stylesheet, resolve BOTH tokens, and compute the ratio: `curl -s https://<domain>/assets/css/styles.css | grep -oE '\-\-color-(primary|surface|text)\s*:\s*#[0-9A-Fa-f]{3,6}'` then a two-line WCAG relative-luminance calculation (the sRGB linearisation matters — a naive RGB distance calls 1.06:1 "different colours"). **Do this per SITE, not per component**: the same template is correct on six of the eight domains it is live on, so a single measurement proves nothing about the others. The second casualty found this way was `mortgagecalculator.co.uk` at **2.95 : 1** (`#b59230` on `#ffffff`), which fails AA and AA-large, on `tool-bridging-compound` and `tool-rate-scenarios`.
- **why it survived:** it can only be caught by looking at the rendered pixels, and the vision half of tool acceptance had **never once run** until 2026-08-11 (`bugs_open/243`). Its first look found this. It then wrote the finding to `doc_notes` category `render-critique`, which **no code reads** (`grep -rn "render-critique" --include=*.go platform/ internal/ pkg/` → 0), while the verdict said `## Tier-4 acceptance PASSED` in the same second — so a second occurrence would be equally invisible today.
- **relations:** `bugs_open/243` (why nothing was looking), the `generic_theme` colour-churn landmine (**distinct — this is NOT palette churn; both tokens hold the values the site intends**), the `var(--x,#fallback)` landmine (that one is about a literal never being applied; this one is about a value applied correctly and meaning the wrong thing).
- **added:** 2026-08-11, staged_component_build lane

### `uq_code_symbols_identity` is `(repo, path, symbol)` and KIND IS NOT IN IT — a newly-indexed kind can overwrite an existing symbol of the same name in the same file, and every total still balances

- **footprint:** `code_symbols` (`uq_code_symbols_identity`, `ON CONFLICT (repo, path, symbol) DO UPDATE`), `platform/orchestration/actions/code_symbols_actions.go` (~line 596, the row-building loop), `internal/analysis/analyse.go` + `types.go` (`ValueDef`, `valueDefs`, the `token.VAR`/`token.CONST` arm), anyone adding a `kind` to `codeKindList` or to the `code_symbols_kind_check` CHECK set
- **fires when:** you teach the analyser to emit a **new kind** of symbol, or you compare the analyser's output count against the row count and try to explain a difference. The unique key does not include `kind`, so a new `var Foo` indexed into a file that already contains `func Foo` **UPSERTs over the func row**: the row survives, its `kind`, `body` and `line_start` become the var's, and the function is gone from the index. Nothing errors, nothing logs, and the row count is unchanged — so a total-rows check reads as healthy.
- **the tell: the per-kind census, and only if you take a BEFORE.** `SELECT kind, count(*) FROM code_symbols GROUP BY 1` taken before and after the first indexing run with the new kind is the whole detector: an old kind's count going **down** is the collision. A total count cannot see it (one row replaced one row) and a spot-check of the new kind cannot either (the new rows are all present and correct — they are the winners).
- **the check, and it is cheaper than the census:** enumerate the collisions directly from the analyser's own output instead of inferring them from counts — build the deployed analyser, walk each file, and intersect the new kind's names against the stored-symbol names already emitted for that file. Measured for `bugs_open/223` phase 2 on 2026-08-11: **0 value-vs-existing collisions**, so nothing was destroyed. **That zero is a fact about one tree on one day, not a property of the schema** — the next kind, or the same kind against a tree that has grown a `var Handler` beside a `func Handler`, gets no such luck.
- **the two traps inside the reconciliation itself**, both of which will make you think you have found a collision when you have not: (1) **methods are immune** — they are stored receiver-qualified as `(*Recv).Name`, so 31 in-file name clashes in this repo cost exactly **0** rows; (2) **plain funcs are not** — two `init()` in one file is legal Go and costs one row every time (`directory_claims.go` and `check_phantom_internal_links.go`, −2 funcs, which is the entire difference between the analyser's 3,702 and the index's 3,700). Reconcile those before calling a delta a defect.
- **relations:** `bugs_open/223` phase 2 (the change that made this reachable), the receiver-qualified-method landmine above (same constraint, opposite direction — that one is about *querying*, this one about *writing*), `internal/analysis`'s blank-identifier skip (`var _ Iface = (*T)(nil)` would otherwise self-collide once per file, which is the same mechanism caught at design time)
- **added:** 2026-08-11, bugfix_223_index_answerability lane

### A change that adds NO new string literal cannot be pod-grepped — but it CAN be dated exactly, and the recipe that says otherwise is now out of date

- **footprint:** any `strings /app/<binary> | grep -c "<marker>"` verification; `makefile` `verify-agent-images`; `cmd/agent-chassis/main.go:53` (`build provenance`); `platform/orchestration/actions/agent_image.go` (`resolveAgentImage`, `chooseAgentImage`, `agentImageIsPinned`); any handoff saying "this change cannot be pod-grepped"
- **fires when:** your change adds behaviour using vocabulary the binary already contained — a new `switch` arm on an existing token, a struct field, a loop over an existing list. `bugs_open/223` phase 2 is the worked case: it made the analyser emit `var` and `const`, but both spellings were already in the binary via `codeKindList`, so the standing pod-grep recipe answers `1` before the change and `1` after and proves nothing in either direction.
- **the tell: a marker count that is identical before and after, which reads as "already shipped".** The old remedy — "date it by a descendant's literal", i.e. find some later commit that *did* add a string and grep for that instead — is indirect, needs a descendant to exist, and proves only that something newer shipped.
- **the check:** ask the pod what it was built from. `kubectl -n ai-persona-system logs <pod> | grep -m1 'build provenance'` prints `{"git_commit":"<40 hex>"}` (`bugs_open/153`, live since v1.0.1283), and `git merge-base --is-ancestor <your-commit> <that-sha>` answers the real question. **Test ANCESTRY, not equality** — the stamp is whatever HEAD was at build time, and one `make release` resolves `HEAD` separately per service, so your commit is normally an ancestor rather than the stamp. Locally: `docker image inspect <img> --format '{{index .Config.Labels "org.opencontainers.image.revision"}}'`.
- **do NOT try to discover the sha from the binary.** `grep -aoE "[0-9a-f]{40}"` on the raw file is unanchored and matches Go's internal digit table, returning `0001020304050607…` on every service with total confidence (`bugs_open/153`, trap 2); and `strings` is **absent from debian-slim images**, so behind the customary `2>/dev/null` it returns a silent 0 that is indistinguishable from "no stamp" (trap 1).
- **for a SPAWNED agent, the chassis pod's stamp is not the answer** — check that pod's own image. `resolveAgentImage` makes a spawned agent inherit the running chassis tag *unless* its `agent_definitions` row sets `default_config.pin_image_tag = true`, in which case it stays on the row's tag through every roll. Verified for `code-indexer` and `landmine-verifier` on 2026-08-11 (neither pinned; both ran `v1.0.1284`).
- **relations:** `bugs_open/153` (the stamp, and both traps), `bugs_open/223` §4a (the handoff this retires), `bugs_open/066` (`agent_definitions.image_tag` trailing the running chassis — the reason `resolveAgentImage` exists at all)
- **added:** 2026-08-11, bugfix_223_index_answerability lane

### The code index is only as fresh as the last PUSH, not the last commit — and a landmine verdict's "cannot verify" reason is manufactured on exactly the symbols you just added

- **footprint:** `code_symbols` (`commit_sha`, `ref`, `commit_time`), `platform/orchestration/actions/diagnose_code_lookup_action.go` (`codeIndexScope`, `missingKindNote`, `kindSummary`, `emptyAnswer`, `unanswerableReason`), `platform/orchestration/actions/analyse_repo_local_action.go` (tarball fetch of the REMOTE ref), `scripts/trigger-landmine-verifier.sh`, `scripts/landmines-verify-dispatch.sh`, any `doc_notes` row in category `landmine-verification`, any diagnosis-loop `code_request`
- **fires when:** you verify a landmine entry, read a landmine verdict, or run any code-index lookup for a symbol added recently. `analyse_repo_local` fetches `tarball/<REF>` — the **remote tip** — so the corpus reflects the last **pushed** commit. This tree commits far more often than it pushes: measured 2026-08-11, the index sat at `5a68d6caf` while the working tree was **246 commits and 88 changed `.go` files** ahead (it was 228 ninety minutes earlier — the gap grows while you read it).
- **the tell: there is none, and the caveat actively points the wrong way.** The lookup's evidence line reports the **extension** census and the **kind** census (`bugs_open/223` phase 1) and says **nothing about staleness**. Handed 0 rows plus a caveat listing only kinds and extensions, a model reaches for a kind or extension explanation, because those are the only two it has. Observed verbatim on 2026-08-11: asked about `ValueDef`, the verifier said it was "of kinds not indexed" — **false**, `ValueDef` is a `struct`, and its three siblings from the same file (`FileInfo`, `FuncDef`, `TypeDef` in `internal/analysis/types.go`) were all indexed at that moment. It was absent because the commit that added it had not been pushed. This is `bugs_open/223`'s own failure mode one level up: 223 was "the index cannot represent this KIND and invents a rename"; this is "the index has not seen this COMMIT and invents a kind".
- **the self-reinforcing part, which is why it bites the careful session hardest:** you write a landmine right after making the change, its footprint names the symbols you just added, and those are precisely the symbols least likely to have been pushed. **The verifier is systematically blindest on exactly the entries most likely to be dispatched.**
- > **⚠ CORRECTED 2026-08-11 (same lane, after the 090 round `520b2f7e` and an `llm_call_log` prompt census): "the caveat actively points the wrong way … those are the only two it has" overstated it.** The lookup DOES state the indexed commit, ref, commit age and "local unpushed work is never visible" on every run (`freshnessBanner`, shipped `87d0bcf97`, `bugs_closed/108` defect A) — and that text WAS in all four `verify` prompts in the window (`prompt_rendered LIKE '%never visible%'` → t). Two things remain true and are the real mechanism: (1) the STALE branch is clock-gated at 48h, so at 17h of wall-clock age the calm FRESH variant rendered while the index was 246 commits behind the tree — commit-DISTANCE staleness is invisible to the pod; (2) the model quoted the vocabulary rendered AT the empty answer (the kind census) and talked past the header caveat a screen above — the distinction did not travel WITH the data. So the fix is answer-site vocabulary, not another banner; the check below is unchanged and remains the only reliable guard for a reader.
- **the check, two commands:** ask the index what it is, and diff it against what you are looking at. `SELECT DISTINCT commit_sha, ref, max(commit_time) OVER () FROM code_symbols;` then `git rev-list --count <that_sha>..HEAD` and `git diff --name-only <that_sha>..HEAD -- '*.go' | wc -l`. If your symbol was added inside that window, a 0-row answer is **your** staleness, not the code's. Confirm the direct way — `git log -S'<symbol>' --oneline | tail -1` gives the commit that introduced it; `git merge-base --is-ancestor <that> <index_sha>` answers whether the index could possibly hold it.
- **do NOT reach for `git rev-parse origin/<branch>`** to find the pushed tip: it reads the local remote-tracking cache and is only as fresh as your last fetch. `git ls-remote origin <branch>` asks the remote.
- **relations:** `bugs_closed/108` (index FRESH while 667 commits behind — **its fix works and this is not a regression of it**: the pin to the live working branch is correct and the refresh runs; this is the residual, that "current with the branch" and "current with the code" are different claims on a tree where commits outpace pushes), `bugs_open/223` phase 1 (the caveat that reports kinds and extensions but not commits), the receiver-qualified-method landmine (a *third* way to get 0 rows for code that exists — check all three before concluding absence)
- **added:** 2026-08-11, bugfix_223_index_answerability lane

### A discovery work item's `created_at` is when the RUN's transaction opened, not when the check filed it — so timing a check by its own item under-reads by the whole run

- **footprint:** `site_work_items.created_at` / `updated_at` (both `DEFAULT now()`), `platform/orchestration/actions/discovery_checks.go:137` (`tx, err := params.DB.BeginTx`) through `:286` (`tx.Commit()`), every `platform/orchestration/actions/discovery_checks/check_*.go`, any query reasoning about *when* a finding was made or how long a check took
- **fires when:** you time a discovery check, order findings within a run, or — the case that produced this entry — reason backwards from an item's timestamp to whether a guard inside the check ran. `run_discovery_checks` opens **one** transaction before the first check executes and commits after the last, and Postgres `now()` is `transaction_timestamp()`, not the statement clock. So every item filed by every check in that run carries the timestamp of the moment the transaction opened, no matter how much probing happened afterwards.
- **the tell: an item that appears to have been created BEFORE the work that created it could have finished** — and it looks exactly like a guard being skipped. Worked case, 2026-08-11 (`bugs_open/236` drill): `check_site_unreachable` files only after a **confirming second probe** separated by a deliberate 5s wait, so an item cannot honestly exist less than ~5s into the check. The filed item's `created_at` was **1.43s** after the orchestration row's `created_at`. That reads as "the confirm-before-filing guard did not run", which would be a real defect in a check whose whole job is not to cry wolf. It had run: the orchestration's own wall time was **7.64s** against **1.8s** for a healthy-path run of the same agent — the ~5.8s delta *is* the retry.
- **the check:** never time a check from its item. Use the orchestration row (`orchestration_states.created_at` → `updated_at`) which brackets the real work, and compare against a known-good run of the same agent so the number has a control. If you genuinely need per-statement time, `clock_timestamp()` is the function that advances inside a transaction; `now()`, `current_timestamp` and `transaction_timestamp()` are all frozen at BEGIN.
- **the same transaction explains a second misleading column:** `created_by` is `params.ExecutionContext.Sender.AgentType` (`discovery_checks.go:132`), which for a **scheduled** dispatch is the scheduler's identity, not the check's agent. The 236 drill's items read `created_by = 'generic'`, not `availability-discovery-agent` — so **`created_by` does not name the producing agent** for anything the rotation drives. `spec->>'check'` does. Same shape as `bugs_open/213`'s lesson that `item_type` hides the producer split.
- **relations:** `bugs_open/236` (the drill that surfaced both), `bugs_open/213` (`spec->>'audit_source'` as the only honest producer name), the memory entry *"a mutation that PASSES may have hit a guard in SERIES"* — this is its mirror: a guard that looks SKIPPED because the instrument, not the guard, was wrong
- **added:** 2026-08-11, bugfix_236_site_availability lane

### Deleting a Cloudflare worker route does NOT fast-fail the apex — it HANGS, and the edge keeps serving 200 for ~30s after the delete and 522 for ~20s after the restore

- **footprint:** `scripts/cloudflare/` (`worker.js`, README), `https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/zones/<zone>/workers/routes`, any `curl` used to confirm a site is up or down during a routing change, `platform/orchestration/actions/discovery_checks/check_site_unreachable.go` (`siteProbeTimeout`)
- **fires when:** you take a site down on purpose (a drill, a migration, a route swap) and use `curl` to decide the change has landed. **Both edges of the change lag, in opposite directions, and both lags look like your change failing.** Measured 2026-08-11 on `cookly.uk` during the `bugs_open/236` drill: the apex answered **200 immediately after the DELETE succeeded**, and answered **522 for ~18s after the re-CREATE succeeded**. A session that curled once after the delete would conclude the delete had not worked and delete something else; a session that curled once after the restore would conclude it had broken the site permanently.
- **the second half, which matters for any availability checker:** with the route gone the apex did not return a fast 5xx — it **hung until the client timed out** (`context deadline exceeded` at the 15s probe timeout). So a reachability check with a short timeout does not merely report a different reason for this failure class, it can **miss the class entirely** if its timeout is under the hang. 15s caught it; a 5s probe might not have.
- **the check:** poll, do not sample — `for i in $(seq 6); do curl -sL --max-time 25 -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://<domain>/; sleep 5; done` — and treat the API's `"success": true` as proof the *API call* worked, never as proof the site's state changed. Always re-list the routes (`GET .../workers/routes`) **and** curl the apex before declaring a restore complete.
- **before you need the write path at all, prove BOTH verbs on a throwaway pattern** (`POST` then `DELETE` a route like `<domain>/__drill-probe-<rand>/*`, which matches nothing real). The token in `~/.cloudflare/404-token.env` turns out to permit worker-route read/write but **NOT** DNS reads, so its scope cannot be guessed from its name — and discovering a missing permission with the site already down is the failure this avoids.
- **relations:** `bugs_open/236` (the drill), `bugs_open/132` (the same token, and the worker whose bindings a careless PUT strips), `bugs_open/153` (the general shape: a successful command is not a shipped change)
- **added:** 2026-08-11, bugfix_236_site_availability lane

### The new "ask the service what it is running" provenance recipe is INOPERATIVE on agent-chassis — its stamp is a STARTUP line and the chassis rotates it away in minutes

- **footprint:** `kubectl logs -l app=agent-chassis … | grep 'build provenance'`, `pkg/buildinfo.GitCommit`, `cmd/agent-chassis/main.go:53`, CLAUDE.md § "Building & deploying images" (the recipe rewritten 2026-08-11), `bugs_open/153`, register **BLD-019**
- **fires when:** you follow the current CLAUDE.md instruction — *"Ask the service what it is running. Do not hunt for markers, and do not use `strings`"* — against the chassis, and get **nothing**. `buildinfo.GitCommit` is logged **once, at startup** (`appLogger.Info("build provenance", …)`). The chassis emits dozens of debug lines per action and its container log rotates on size, so on a pod more than a few minutes old the stamp is already gone. Measured 2026-08-11: pods started 09:23Z, and at 10:07Z `logs --since=24h | grep -c "build provenance"` returned **0** on both replicas — not "unstamped", *rotated*. The recipe is sound for quiet services and silently useless for the noisiest one, which is also the one most often verified.
- **the trap inside the trap — the obvious fallback is WORSE.** Reaching for the sanctioned binary probe (`grep -aq "<sha>" /proc/1/exe`) with **your own commit's sha** returns absent on a binary that genuinely contains your change: the binary is stamped with **ONE** commit — the build point — not with every ancestor. Three absents in a row (including what you thought were positive controls) reads as "my fix did not ship" and is actually "wrong test". The stamp is a single value you must first *obtain*, then compare with `git merge-base --is-ancestor <your-commit> <the stamp>`. Note this also means you cannot use a commit you know is present as a positive control unless it IS the stamp.
- **the check:** for the chassis, **prefer behaviour over provenance** — fire the smallest input that only the new code can answer and read the outcome (a witness agent, an induced rejection, a filed row). It proves the code is *running*, which provenance never does. If you need the stamp itself, get it from the image rather than the pod (`docker pull <image>` then probe the extracted binary for specific candidate shas, each with a must-be-absent control) — never a discovery grep for "some 40-hex string", which matches Go's internal digit table. And when a pod IS young enough, grab the stamp immediately: `kubectl logs <pod> | head -1` tells you whether the log even reaches back to startup.
- **relations:** the existing *"Chassis pod logs rotate away within MINUTES"* entry (same rotation, different consequence — that one is about missing an event, this one about missing your own build identity); `bugs_open/249` (one release tag shipping three source revisions, so the stamp is per-SERVICE); the memory entry *"a believable OUTAGE explaining a NULL is when to doubt the INSTRUMENT"*, which is the general form
- **REFINED 2026-08-13 (silent_hero_logo_readers lane) — "INOPERATIVE" is too strong: it is TIME-LIMITED, and this entry already contains the test that tells you which case you are in.** Measured on `v1.0.1295`: pods started `13:53:19Z`, and at `14:00:23Z` — **7 minutes** — `logs --tail=100000 | grep -m1 'build provenance'` returned the stamp cleanly. **This entry's own precheck is the discriminator and belongs FIRST, not as a footnote:** `kubectl logs <pod> | head -1` showing a startup line means the log still reaches back and the stamp is in range; anything else means it does not. So the operative rule is **ask immediately after a roll and prove the window**, not "skip the recipe on this service". Both readings are dangerous in opposite directions — "it works" invites a false negative hours later, "it never works" sends you to the `strings`/`/proc/1/exe` trap in the bullet above when a one-command exact answer was there for the taking. The ancestry comparison stays mandatory either way: the stamp is ONE commit and never yours, so `git merge-base --is-ancestor <your-commit> <stamp>` plus a descendant as a must-be-absent control
- **added:** 2026-08-11, bugfix_234_dead_spec_key lane; **refined 2026-08-13, silent_hero_logo_readers lane**

### `099_SYNC_gate_roster.py --apply` now SILENTLY REVERTS migration 377 — it regenerates all 17 gate prompts and its transform predates the cache breakpoint, so the mirror CLAUDE.md tells you to run destroys a proven 68% saving

- **footprint:** `docs/agent_docs/docs024_key_docs_latest/fixloop_eg_dartsonline/099_SYNC_gate_roster.py` (`transform_step`, the drift compare), `docs/agent_docs/sql_for_agents/377_council_gate_cache_breakpoint_reorder.sql`, `platform/aiservice/anthropic.go` (`CacheBreakpointMarker`), `agent_definitions` rows `council-gate` and `fix-proposer` (`default_config->workflow->steps->review_*`), CLAUDE.md's "If you add or change a council seat … run the mirror — do not hand-patch the gate"
- **fires when:** you add or change a council seat and follow CLAUDE.md's instruction to mirror. Migration **377** hoisted the 172-char shared evidence block (schema + rationale + plan) to the **front** of all 17 `council-gate` seats and inserted `<!--CACHE_BREAKPOINT-->` after it, because Anthropic caching is a **PREFIX** match and each seat's persona previously pushed the shared body to a different offset — measured common prefix **zero characters**. `099`'s `transform_step` was written before that and rebuilds each gate prompt from `fix-proposer` in the **old** order, with no marker. `--apply` therefore reverts 377 across all 17 seats and takes the caching with it: **68% measured saving in production**, on the subsystem that was ~85% of all fleet LLM spend.
- **the tell is there and it reads as the opposite of what it means.** The dry run prints `drift (steps that would change): [all 17 review_* steps]` while `added: (none) removed: (none)`. That looks like "the gate has drifted badly, mirror it" — it is in fact "the gate is AHEAD of the mirror". Confirmed 2026-08-11 by diffing one seat nobody had touched (`review_mission`): the only difference was 377's hoist. Compare lengths and you get the same answer in one query — every untouched gate seat is **exactly +37 chars** (marker + newlines) against its `fix-proposer` twin, which is 377's arithmetic, not divergence.
- **the check, before any `--apply`:** `SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE s.value->'config'->>'prompt_template' LIKE '%<!--CACHE_BREAKPOINT-->%'), count(DISTINCT md5(split_part(s.value->'config'->>'prompt_template','<!--CACHE_BREAKPOINT-->',1))) FROM agent_definitions a, jsonb_each(a.default_config->'workflow'->'steps') s WHERE a.type='council-gate' AND a.is_active AND COALESCE(a.is_snapshot,false)=false AND a.deleted_at IS NULL AND s.key LIKE 'review_%';` — **17 and 1** is healthy: every seat marked, and one SHARED prefix. Run it again after. A prefix count above 1 means caching has silently stopped paying even though every seat still carries a marker.
- **what to do instead, until `099` learns about 377:** apply the seat change to `fix-proposer` by migration as usual, then mirror it into `council-gate` with a **second, surgical migration anchored on a verbatim line**, guarded to abort if the breakpoint moves or the shared prefix fragments. `381` (fix-proposer) + `383` (gate) are the worked pair. **This is a deliberate, documented exception to CLAUDE.md's "do not hand-patch the gate", not permission to ignore it** — that rule exists because two hand-maintained rosters drift, and it assumes the mirror is faithful. It is not, today, and obeying its letter would cause exactly the regression it exists to prevent. **Fix `099` and this exception ends.**
- **why the guard belongs in the migration and not in your head:** insert your text **after** the breakpoint and the cached prefix is untouched; insert it before and you invalidate the cache for all 17 seats while every seat still looks correctly marked. `383` asserts `position(marker)` is unchanged and refuses if the anchor precedes the marker — one `RAISE`, and it is the only thing standing between a routine prompt edit and a silent bill.
- **relations:** `council_gate_cost` lane (377's own workstream and the 68% measurement), `RFC_022` (the seat change that surfaced this), the migration-verify landmine (**377 and 383 both verify by `RAISE`, not by `SELECT`** — under `ON_ERROR_STOP` a non-empty result set does not abort, so a `SELECT`-shaped verify block lets a failed migration COMMIT and report success)
- **added:** 2026-08-11, bugfix_223_index_answerability lane, implementing the RFC_022 ruling

### A decomposition lane's `page_components_bak_*` re-captures on EVERY run, so it holds two generations per page and `--restore` replays both onto one page

- **footprint:** `docs024_key_docs_latest/loanandmortgagecalculator_couk/load_lmc.py` (`backup_everything`, `--restore`), `docs024_key_docs_latest/loancalculator_couk/decompose/load_decomposition.py` (same code, **STILL DEFECTIVE**), tables `page_components_bak_20260805_lmc` and `page_components_bak_20260802_decomp`, `bugs_open/250`
- **fires when:** you convert pages one at a time — which is what every runbook here tells you to do — and later reach for the per-page rollback. The backup INSERT guards **per ROW** (`NOT EXISTS … b.id = pc.id`), so once a page is decomposed the *next* `--apply` of **any** page sees that page's new `prose-0` row as "not yet backed up" and copies it in **beside** its original `ported-page` row. `--restore` then does `DELETE … ; INSERT … SELECT * FROM <bak>` and puts **both generations back on one page** — a whole verbatim document *and* a prose section, which is the nested-`<html>` corruption `load_lmc.py`'s own docstring warns about, arriving through the safety net. `--restore` exits 0 and prints `restored <page>`. Nothing is wrong until the page renders.
- **the check, before you trust any rollback in these lanes:** `SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT page_id FROM <bak> GROUP BY page_id HAVING count(*) FILTER (WHERE slot_name='ported-page') > 0 AND count(*) FILTER (WHERE slot_name <> 'ported-page') > 0) x;` — **must be 0**. `SELECT count(*), count(DISTINCT page_id) FROM <bak>;` must be equal, and the cheap tell is that they are not. Measured 2026-08-11: LMC **42 rows / 41 pages**, loancalculator **28 / 27**, one poisoned rollback each.
- **the trap inside the trap — the SAME function is also broken by schema drift, in the direction you will not test.** The table is cloned `LIKE page_components INCLUDING ALL` on day one; `page_components` has since gained `rendered_html_digest`, so `SELECT pc.*` is 28 expressions into 27 columns and the **backup** dies with *"INSERT has more expressions than target columns"*. The **restore** direction is fine — fewer expressions than target columns is legal SQL and the trailing ones take their defaults — so **drift breaks the backup loudly and the restore not at all**. A session that exercises only `--restore` concludes the rollback is healthy while no new backup has been written since the column landed. Check `(SELECT count(*) FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name='page_components') = (… WHERE table_name='<bak>')` before believing either half.
- **why it stayed invisible for six days:** the poisoning is written by a *successful* run and read only by a rollback nobody performs on a good day. It began on 2026-08-05 and was found on 08-11 only because `--apply` refused to start — it backs up **first**, so it failed *before* writing anything. **A tool that fails safe told us something a tool that succeeded would not have**; had the column landed in the other order, Track A would have converted 17 pages and poisoned 16 rollbacks in silence.
- **the general form, worth carrying to any backup you did not watch work:** *a store that re-captures on every run is a LOG, not a SNAPSHOT.* A rollback source needs exactly **one generation per subject**, so its guard must key on the **subject** (`page_id`), never on the **row**. And prove it the only way that counts — apply, restore, assert the stored md5 equals a recorded baseline, re-apply. Believing an untested rollback is the whole of this entry.
- **relations:** `bugs_open/250` (the case, with the close-out steps for the sibling lane), `bugs_open/204`/`189` (why a decomposed page must hold exactly one generation of rows), the memory entry *"a `complete` work item is not a repaired artefact"* (same family: the status is not the artefact), and the migration-verify landmine — the repair here uses `DO`/`RAISE`, because a verify block of bare `SELECT`s cannot stop the `COMMIT`
- **added:** 2026-08-11, loanandmortgagecalculator_couk Track A lane

### The council verdict note you read with `ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 1` is very likely ANOTHER LANE'S — the gate is fleet-wide and rounds interleave

- **footprint:** `SELECT body FROM doc_notes WHERE categories ? 'council-gate' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 1` (the query printed by `097_TRIGGER_council_review_v1.sh` and quoted in `RUNBOOK_council_gate.md`), `diagnosis_artifacts` kind=`council_report`, any "did my submission pass?" question
- **fires when:** your round is still executing and you read the newest note. ~30 sessions share this gate and several submit per hour, so the newest `council-gate` note is whichever lane finished most recently — **not yours**. Measured 2026-08-11: with my round mid-flight at `review_architecture`, that exact query returned a confident **APPROVED** whose summary was about `build-dispatch-loop`'s `purpose?` input_mapping and migration 380 — a different lane's change entirely. The failure is silent and flattering: it hands you an APPROVED verdict with a plausible-looking summary, and the only tell is reading the summary carefully enough to notice it describes work you did not do.
- **why the obvious guard is not enough:** the trigger tells you to save `SUBMISSION_CORR` and the note *contains* it — but the query it prints does not FILTER on it, so having the correlation saved does not protect you. On a resubmission the trap is worse: the correlation is REUSED across rounds, so even a correctly-filtered `LIMIT 1` can hand you the **previous round's** verdict (mine returned round 1's REJECTED while round 2 was still running) — which reads as "the resubmission failed" when it has not finished.
- **the check:** filter by your correlation AND confirm your run is finished first, in that order:
  ```sql
  -- 1. is MY round actually done? (find the run by payload, per the runbook)
  SELECT current_step, status FROM orchestration_states
   WHERE collected_data->'input_data'->>'fix_correlation_id' = '<SUBMISSION_CORR>'
   ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 1;          -- must be COMPLETED, not EXECUTING_STEP
  -- 2. only then, and always correlation-filtered:
  SELECT created_at, body FROM doc_notes
   WHERE categories ? 'council-gate' AND body LIKE '%<SUBMISSION_CORR>%'
   ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 3;          -- LIMIT 3, so a resubmission's rounds are visible as a series
  ```
  A `complete_invalid` run is a third state to recognise: the submission was refused by `diagnose_persist_fix_plan` before any seat ran, so it produces **no note at all** — and `error` is NULL with `execution_path` empty (the `bugs_open/099` shape). No note plus an empty execution path means *nothing was reviewed*, not *nothing was wrong*.
- **relations:** `RUNBOOK_council_gate.md` (whose printed query this corrects), the memory entry *"a gate's 0 findings has TWO causes, opposite fixes"*, `bugs_open/099` (failed step reads COMPLETED with error NULL)
- **added:** 2026-08-11, bugfix_234_dead_spec_key lane

### Patching `page_components.content_data` is invisible to the page — assembly reads STORED `rendered_html`

- **footprint:** `page_components.content_data`, `page_components.rendered_html`,
  `item_type='page_rerender'`, `rerender_single_page`
- **fires when:** correcting a value in a page component's `content_data` (a URL,
  a figure, a name) and firing a `page_rerender` to ship it. The item completes,
  the page redeploys, `deployed_at` moves — and the served page is unchanged,
  because a `page_rerender` ASSEMBLES the page from each component's stored
  `rendered_html`; it does not re-render components from `content_data`.
  (Site-chrome variant already known from 08-10: `refresh_site_components`
  exists precisely because plain rerenders reuse chrome. This is the
  page-component face — there is no equivalent refresh flag.)
- **the tell:** none per-run — completed item, fresh deploy timestamp, changed
  nothing. Only grepping the SERVED page for the corrected value catches it
- **the check:** patch BOTH halves in one UPDATE (`content_data` so future real
  re-renders inherit the truth, `rendered_html` so assembly serves it), back up
  the row first, then rerender and grep the served page:
  `curl -s https://<domain>/<page> | grep -o '<the corrected value>'`
- **source:** hit directly, fundamentallyai portfolio hot-link repair 2026-08-11
  (NOTES_209 08-11 section); mechanism first recorded for chrome in NOTES_209
  08-10 ("the re-render step took THREE attempts")
- **added:** 2026-08-11, bugfix_209_deploy_purpose_keyed_source lane

### A bucket-only edit to a repo-backed site is PROVISIONAL — the next domain deploy restores the repo's version, and `--skip-newer` does not protect you

- **footprint:** `b2://portfolio-sites/<domain>/` · `gqls/sites` (the sites repo) · `b2 file upload … portfolio-sites` · `.github` "Deploy to B2" action (`034_github_action.md:68`) · any fix applied to a served file rather than to what WRITES the served file
- **fires when:** you correct a live page by editing the bucket object — the natural move, it is where the bytes serve from, and every verification you run (origin re-download, edge fetch, byte count) passes. The fix is real and complete **until the next push touching that domain**, when `b2 sync --delete --skip-newer <domain> b2://portfolio-sites/<domain>` replays the repo's copy over yours.
- **the tell — `--skip-newer` LOOKS like protection and is not:** it compares modification times, and **a fresh checkout stamps every repo file with checkout time**, so the repo copy is always "newer" than your bucket edit no matter when either was really written. The flag protects against nothing in this pipeline. `--delete` additionally removes any bucket file with no repo counterpart, so a bucket-only *addition* dies the same way.
- **the check:** after any bucket-side fix, ask **what writes this store** and fix that too, in the same task: `gh api repos/gqls/sites/contents/<domain>/<path> --jq '.size,.sha'` — if the size is the OLD size, the fix has a countdown on it. Both stores in one task, verified independently. And the converse when deleting: a bucket delete of a repo-backed file is undone by the next sync; delete in the repo (`gh api -X DELETE …/contents/… -f sha=…`) or it resurrects.
- **why it is a landmine:** the failure is time-delayed and attributed to nobody. The sync that undoes you is triggered by an unrelated session's unrelated commit, days later; the regression looks like *your fix never happened*, and nothing links it to the deploy that reverted it. Measured live 2026-08-11: the mortgagecalculator backlink removal (bucket-only, 08-10, fully verified at origin AND edge) sat one push away from silent reversal — the repo still held the 11,125-byte backlinked `index.html`. Caught only because a rejected image's deletion forced the "what writes this store" question a day later. Both fixed in the repo (`565733ac`, `a1963dc5`); the triggered deploys then converged both stores, deleting nothing (52 files before and after — measured, not assumed).
- **source:** 2026-08-11, `bugfix_210_needs_logo_unhandleable` lane; `WRONG_CALLS.md` same date
- **added:** 2026-08-11, bugfix_210 lane

### A workflow step's NAME is not its ACTION — a config read through the action name returns NULL, indistinguishable from "the key was never added"

- **footprint:** `agent_definitions.default_config->'workflow'->'steps'` · any `SELECT … ->'steps'->'<name>'->'config'->>'<key>'` · `request_run` (action `request_browser_run`) · `look` (action `execute_vision_prompt`) · verifying a config-only migration landed
- **fires when:** you verify a DB-config change by reading the step you know by its ACTION name — which is the name the Go code, the bug files and every handoff use, because that is what identifies the behaviour. The step KEY is chosen by whoever seeded the agent and is often shorter: `tool-acceptance-agent`'s browser-run step is keyed **`request_run`**, and its vision step **`look`**. Reading `steps->'request_browser_run'->…` returns NULL for every key you ask for.
- **the tell that is NOT a tell:** `? '<key>'` returns NULL too, and so does `jsonb_pretty()` of the whole config — so the "enumerate keys, don't path-read" habit still fails if you enumerate keys of a step that does not exist. Three reads agreeing on NULL feels like confirmation; they are one mistake three times ([[two-blind-checks-agree-with-each-other]] shape).
- **the check:** enumerate the STEP names first, every time, before reading anything inside one — `SELECT jsonb_object_keys(default_config->'workflow'->'steps') FROM agent_definitions WHERE type='<t>' AND is_active AND COALESCE(is_snapshot,false)=false AND deleted_at IS NULL;` — then map action→step with `SELECT k, v->>'action' FROM …, LATERAL jsonb_each(default_config->'workflow'->'steps') s(k,v)`. A NULL config read is only evidence once you have proven the step key exists.
- **why it is a landmine:** the wrong result is the *plausible* one. On 2026-08-11 this made migration 384 (`url_field` on tool-acceptance) read as **not applied** minutes after another session had applied and verified it — a false "the fix is missing" about a live change, which is the direction that costs a duplicate implementation. The key was present all along with `input_data.spec.page_url`.
- **source:** 2026-08-11, `staged_component_build` lane (NOTES 08-11 afternoon; the wrapper `page_url` work)
- **added:** 2026-08-11, staged_component_build lane

## A CTA fix written only to `rendered_html` is invisible to the template — the next content_data-driven rerender silently drops it

- **footprint:** `page_components.content_data` · `page_components.rendered_html` ·
  `content_components.html_template` · any hero/CTA component using
  `{{if and .cta_text .cta_url}}` · `pages.sections` (rebuild membership) ·
  `scheduled_tasks.improvement-sweep`
- **fires when:** you resolve an `unresolved_cta`/`cta_names_unknown_destination`
  finding by writing the button's `href` straight into `rendered_html` (the fast,
  obvious fix — it's what's actually served, and `verify_served_site.sh` goes
  green immediately)
- **the tell:** **there is no tell at the time you make the fix.** It looks
  completely correct: the live page shows the button, the check passes, the
  work item can be marked resolved. The gap only shows up later, on the NEXT
  event that regenerates `rendered_html` FROM `content_data` — a
  `refresh_site_components` rerender, a component-template fixer pass, a fresh
  `improvement-sweep` cycle — because the hero template's own guard is
  `{{if and .cta_text .cta_url}}`. `content_data` had `cta_text` but never
  `cta_url` (only `rendered_html` did), so the regenerated HTML drops the
  button silently — no error, no failed check, just an empty pair of blank
  lines where the button used to be. Hit directly, twice, same incident,
  2026-08-11: `webdesign.uk`'s hero CTAs on `index.html` and `contact.html`
  both reverted this way roughly 20 hours after being "fixed", and a **third**,
  worse case in the same incident: `contact.html`'s hand-built
  `chat-input-box` component was never added to `pages.sections` at all when
  it was spliced in, so a sections-driven rebuild didn't just drop a field —
  it dropped the entire component, silently, because the component was never
  on the list of things to keep
- **the check:** before considering a CTA/component fix durable, verify the
  URL lives in **`content_data`**, not only `rendered_html` —
  `SELECT content_data->>'cta_url', content_data->>'secondary_cta_url' FROM
  page_components WHERE id=…` must be non-null if the template's guard needs
  both fields. For a hand-inserted, framework-external component (no template
  describes it, nothing should ever regenerate it), the durable fix is
  different in kind, not degree: **lock it**
  (`UPDATE page_components SET locked_at=now(), lock_type='permanent' WHERE
  id=…`) AND add it to `pages.sections`, or the next full rebuild has no
  record it should exist and silently omits it — a lock protects the ROW,
  the sections array is what decides whether the row is even considered
- **the mechanism underneath, worth knowing before you next touch
  `improvement-sweep`:** it can be re-enabled by something other than the
  session that disabled it, with no announcement — `scheduled_tasks.enabled`
