### `kubectl run -i --rm … kcat -P < file` drops roughly 4 publishes in 5 AT EXIT 0 — and with both streams discarded there is no receipt in either direction, so a lost dispatch looks exactly like queue latency

- **footprint:** `kubectl run -i` · `kcat -P` · `docs/leopardessconsulting/scripts/commit_brand_assets.sh` · `docs/leopardessconsulting/scripts/rerender_pages.sh` · `brochure_component_library/scripts/deploy_stylesheet_direct.sh` · `scripts/initial_messages/**` · any hand-dispatch that pipes or redirects a payload into a `kubectl run -i` container
- **fires when:** you reuse a *proven, documented* publish script from a site lane. Nothing about it looks suspect: it has a header explaining the contract, it has worked before, and it exits 0 every time — including the times it published nothing.
- **the trap:** `kubectl run -i` wires stdin **asynchronously** to a container that is already starting. If the container reaches `kcat` before stdin is attached, kcat sees EOF, publishes zero messages and exits 0. Measured 2026-07-26: **four of five publishes lost.** Most of these scripts then send stdout and stderr to `/dev/null`, so there is no evidence either way — you get an id printed by the *shell*, not by the publisher, and an empty `orchestration_states` five minutes later that reads as ordinary fleet latency.
- **why the wrong result looks exactly like the right one:** a missing orchestration row is the documented signature of *latency* on this cluster (CLAUDE.md tells you not to retry on that evidence), so the correct response to a genuine drop and the correct response to a slow queue are opposites, and the two are indistinguishable at the point you have to choose. Retrying costs a duplicate; waiting costs the whole dispatch.
- **the check — make the PUBLISHER speak, not the shell.** Put the payload in the container **COMMAND** and chain a receipt: base64 the single-line JSON, then `--command -- sh -c "echo '<b64>' | base64 -d | kcat -P … && echo PUBLISH_OK"`. No `PUBLISH_OK` means nothing was published; re-run immediately. Worked implementations: `docs/leopardessconsulting/scripts/rerender_page_safe.sh` (orchestration topic) and `docs/leopardessconsulting/scripts/commit_site_file.sh` (git-adapter topic, register **DGH-009**).
- **⚠ `--command` is itself load-bearing:** the `edenhill/kcat` image's ENTRYPOINT is kcat, so without `--command` your `sh -c …` arrives as *arguments to kcat* and nothing is published — the same silent zero, reached a different way.
- **and keep it to ONE line:** the base64 form also protects you from the separate multi-line trap above (`kcat -P` publishes one message per LINE), which a pretty-printed heredoc walks straight into.
- **source:** measured 2026-07-26 on the leopardess lane (4/5 lost) and re-hit 2026-08-15 as one half of the `075_trigger_discovery.sh` entry above; the safe form was used for a live publish 2026-08-16 (git-adapter corr `142c4a2b`, sitemap.xml)
- **relations:** the `kcat -P` one-message-per-line entry above (different mechanism, same silent-zero outcome) · `075_trigger_discovery.sh` entry · register `DGH-009` · MEMORY [[kcat-publish-silently-drops]] · [[a-post-fix-zero-needs-a-demand-control]]
- **added:** 2026-08-16, leopardess sitemap lane
- **verifier verdict 2026-08-16 (`0392773c`): NEEDS_HUMAN_REVIEW — and it means "cannot check", not "doubtful".** The landmine-verifier's code index holds `.go` files only (7,358 symbols, 0 non-Go), so every footprint here is unanswerable by it; its note asks a human to confirm the named scripts still exist. **Done in the same session, by reading each one:** `commit_brand_assets.sh:93` and `rerender_pages.sh:24` both use `kubectl -n kafka run -i --rm … kcat -P` with the payload on stdin and (in `rerender_pages.sh`) `>/dev/null 2>&1`; `brochure_component_library/scripts/deploy_stylesheet_direct.sh:75` uses the same `run -i` form piped from `printf` (it adds `kcat -P -c 1` and keeps its output, so it has a partial receipt — the stdin race is unaffected). Treat this as a gap in the verifier's reach, not evidence about the entry.

## Re-running an "idempotent" migration takes a SECOND `snapshot_agent` whose reason still says `pre-update` but whose CONTENT is post-change — so "the latest snapshot" is the WRONG pre-image, and the `UPDATE 0` that proves the fence held is exactly what makes it look safe

- **footprint:** `snapshot_agent(text,text)` / `snapshot_agent(text)` · `agent_definitions_backup` · any `docs/agent_docs/sql_for_agents/*.sql` that opens `BEGIN; SELECT snapshot_agent(...)` before a fenced `UPDATE` · any rollback recipe reading `ORDER BY snapshot_taken_at DESC LIMIT 1` · any `INSERT INTO doc_notes` at the tail of a migration
- **fires when:** you re-run a migration on purpose (to re-read scrolled output, to confirm it applied, because two sessions both applied it) and read `UPDATE 0` as "no harm done — the fence held". The fence only guards the statement it is attached to. **Every statement OUTSIDE the fence fires again**, and on this estate's house style that is at least two: the `snapshot_agent` call at the top and the `doc_notes` INSERT at the bottom.
- **the tell — there isn't one, and the inversion is the damage.** The replay's snapshot row is written with the SAME `snapshot_reason` string (`…: pre-update`), so a reader sorting by `snapshot_taken_at DESC` gets a row that is labelled *pre-update* and *contains the post-update config*. `[MEASURED 2026-08-16, migration 417]`: two rows 25 s apart, `15:58:18Z has_old=t / has_new=f` (the real pre-image), `15:58:43Z has_old=f / has_new=t` (the replay's). A hand restore from "the latest snapshot" would have restored the change it was meant to undo, silently and with a verify block that passes. The `doc_notes` INSERT produced a straight duplicate — cheaper, but it consumes a slot in `load_doc_context`'s newest-N window, so the pipeline reading those notes sees one fewer distinct note.
- **the check:** never ask for the newest backup row — **ask for the row that HOLDS the pre-change value**, which cannot lie about its own content: `SELECT snapshot_taken_at, snapshot_reason FROM agent_definitions_backup WHERE type='<agent>' AND default_config #> '{…path…}' ? '<the old key>' ORDER BY snapshot_taken_at DESC LIMIT 1;`. And when you write a migration, **fence every statement, not just the UPDATE** — `INSERT INTO doc_notes (...) SELECT ... WHERE NOT EXISTS (...)`, and either make the snapshot conditional or state in the header that a replay adds a decoy row. "Idempotent" that covers only the UPDATE is not idempotent; the header's own claim is what stops the next reader checking.
- **relations:** LANDMINES "`snapshot_agent` has TWO overloads writing to TWO different tables" (same table, the other half of the trap: that entry already says *don't ask whether a snapshot exists, ask whether it holds the pre-change config* — this is why, and 417's own header got it wrong first time despite citing that entry) · LANDMINES "A `*_TRIGGER_*`/`*_DISPATCH_*`/`*_SUBMIT_*` script … PUBLISHES on every invocation" (the same "re-running a thing to re-read it" habit, one layer up) · `417_image_build_handler_asset_id_goes_strict_HOLD.sql` (header carries the corrected check + the applied record)
- **added:** 2026-08-16, staged_component_build lane (found on 417's own apply — the owner ran it twice)
- **CONTRIBUTED 2026-08-16, portfolio_positioning lane — the DRY-RUN-then-apply discipline does NOT produce the decoy, and three council seats independently thought it did.** It matters because the two workflows look identical from the outside (two `snapshot_agent` calls, one reason string, two rows) and only one is dangerous. A dry run is the same file with `COMMIT` swapped for `ROLLBACK`: the snapshot autocommits, then the **UPDATE is rolled back**, so the second (real) run's snapshot still sees the PRE-change config. `[MEASURED 2026-08-16 across three migrations, using this entry's own content-not-recency check: 433's two `…: pre-update` rows both hold `Directory rule:` = **f**; 434's two both hold **32** checks (post-change is 43); 441's two both hold its new clause = **f**.]` **The decoy needs a replay of an ALREADY-SUCCEEDED apply** — that is 417's case (the owner ran it twice), not the dry-run case. Two cheap consequences: (1) a migration whose pre-flight **refuses when already applied** cannot produce the decoy at all, because the replay aborts before the UPDATE — worth writing that guard for this reason alone, on top of the usual one; (2) when you DO find duplicate `pre-update` rows, do not assume the newest is poisoned — run the content check and find out, because a session that wrongly distrusts its own good snapshot has lost its restore path just as surely as one that trusts a bad one.

### A `090` diagnosis of an oversized-state bug comes back **REFUTED** because the evidence bundle TRUNCATED the very keys it went looking for — the verdict cites the absence as a finding, and reads exactly like a real refutation

- **footprint:** `090_TRIGGER_needs_diagnosis_v1.sh` · `collected_data->'verdict'` / `->'diagnosis'` on any `diagnose-agent` run · `orchestration_states.collected_data` · any hypothesis whose evidence lives IN `collected_data` (loop aggregates, `_iter_<N>_*` keys, `audit_result`, `iteration_results`, large LLM payloads) · `owner_agent_type` `tool-auditor` / `build-dispatch-loop` / `tool-suggester`
- **fires when:** you do the disciplined thing. You have a cross-cutting hypothesis, so you file a `090` rather than asserting it (CLAUDE.md tells you to), you author the symptom properly — mechanism stated, tables and symbols pointed at, no counts asserted — and the verdict comes back **REFUTED** with a specific, quotable, confident reason. If the rows in question are large, that reason may be entirely fabricated out of a truncated bundle.
- **the mechanism, measured 2026-08-16 (`bugs_open/289`):** the loop's bundle cannot carry a 20 MB `collected_data`, so the key enumeration handed to the diagnoser is cut short — and the diagnoser reports the cut as an absence. Run `12ffad7c-a7b2-4955-b531-554f07650598` refuted a *correct* hypothesis with: *"the actual collected_data for orchestration 1a70fed3 … enumerates keys action, llm_audit, load_tool, … item_created_0 through item_created_8 … **and no '_done' key appears at all**."* That row has **ten** `_done` keys, sized 20 kB → 10 MB. An earlier run on the same target (`815322b9…`) failed one step sooner and cited *"(no orchestration rows for this correlation/site)"* against a target with 63 rows. **Two runs, two different false absences, same cause.** Note the recursion in the trap: the bug IS oversized state, so the bug disables the tool you would use to find it.
- **the tell:** the verdict's own citation is an **absence** (`no X appears`, `no rows for`, `does not exist as described`) rather than a value that contradicts you — and the target rows are big. A genuine refutation shows you a row whose *content* disagrees (run `815322b9…` also did this correctly once: it killed a truncation hypothesis by producing a truncated run that had reached `complete`). **An absence quoted from a bundle is not evidence; it is the bundle's own limit.**
- **the check:** before accepting any REFUTED whose reasoning rests on something not being there, re-ask that one question at the DB in a form the bundle cannot distort — a **count**, not a dump: `SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM jsonb_object_keys(collected_data) k WHERE k LIKE '%\_done') FROM orchestration_states WHERE orchestration_id='<the row the verdict names>';`. It costs seconds and it is decisive. On these rows, **never** `SELECT collected_data`, `jsonb_pretty(...)` or `jsonb_each` without a `key LIKE` filter — a single row is up to 29 MB and the query times out at 120 s, which is its own false signal (a timeout reads as "the cluster is busy", not "this row is enormous"). Size first: `SELECT pg_size_pretty(length(collected_data::text)::bigint) FROM …`.
- **relations:** LANDMINES "A census over `workflow.steps.*.action` is BLIND to every action nested in a `sub_workflow`" (same family — a well-formed short answer that omits what you asked about; that entry's remedy, reconcile against a text control, is the same move) · `MEMORY/measurement-discipline-index.md` "interrogating what doesn't EXIST returns a well-formed answer" · `bugs_open/289` (the bug this was found on; its ADDENDUM has both false verdicts quoted in full) · CLAUDE.md "Diagnosis before debugging" — this does **not** argue against filing a `090`; the first run correctly killed a wrong hypothesis. It argues for reading the verdict's citation TYPE before acting on it.
- **added:** 2026-08-16, `bugfix_281_tool_audit_ported` lane (found while taking that lane's handoff forward)

### A loop's `<loop>_iter_<N>_done` key is NOT iteration N's result — it is a full aggregate of the WHOLE loop, so reading one to see what one iteration did hands you every iteration, nested

- **footprint:** `orchestration_states.collected_data` keys matching `_iter_<N>_done` (or any substep declared `action: loop_complete`) · `platform/orchestration/actions/loop_actions.go:LoopCompleteAction` · `platform/orchestration/loop_expansion_handler.go:handleLoopExpansion` · debugging any of the **15 live loops** that carry a `loop_complete` substep (`build-dispatch-loop`, `tool-auditor`, `tool-suggester`, `internal-linker`, `page-rebuild`, `pageflow-builder`, `site-work-orchestrator`, `rerender-site`, `maintenance-triage`, `business-intel`, `component-quality-auditor`, `content-feed-trigger`, `model-directory-trigger`, `vet-batch-processor`, plus `site-work-orchestrator`'s second loop)
- **fires when:** you debug a loop by reading the iteration that went wrong — `collected_data->'create_items_loop_iter_3_done'` — expecting iteration 3's outcome. You get a `results` array covering **all** iterations (including ones that had not run yet, because the injected substep inherits `loop_metadata.total_iterations`), each entry carrying the earlier iterations' own aggregates nested inside it. Iteration 3's data IS in there, which is why the wrong reading survives: you find what you came for and never notice the rest.
- **the mechanism:** the sub-workflow's terminal substep (conventionally `done`) is declared `action: loop_complete` and gets injected once per iteration, so the whole-loop aggregator runs inside every lap. `bugs_open/289` — it is also why `collected_data` doubles per iteration and why `tool-auditor` is dead at 22 MB.
- **the check:** read the per-iteration substep outputs instead — `item_created_<N>`, or `<loop>_iter_<N>_<substep>` for the specific substep — which are genuinely per-iteration. If you must read a `_done`, take `->'results'->N` and ignore its nested `done` key. Sanity-check with sizes: `SELECT key, length(value::text) FROM orchestration_states, jsonb_each(collected_data) WHERE orchestration_id='…' AND key LIKE '%\_done' ORDER BY key;` — **a doubling series means you are looking at nested aggregates, not results.**
- **relations:** `bugs_open/289` · LANDMINES "A `090` diagnosis of an oversized-state bug comes back REFUTED …" (directly above; found together) · `bugs_closed/173` (the other loop-engine defect — error routing granularity; different bug, same files)
- **added:** 2026-08-16, `bugfix_281_tool_audit_ported` lane

### A checks-array enablement migration applies CLEANLY against a binary that does not have the check — the registry SKIPS an unregistered name instead of erroring, so `UPDATE 1` and a longer array are what "enabled but permanently silent" looks like

- **footprint:** `platform/orchestration/actions/discovery_checks/`, `docs/agent_docs/sql_for_agents/`, `completeness-discovery-agent`, `run_checks`, `agent_definitions.default_config`
- **also fires on** (prose, not footprints): the `checks` array at `{workflow,steps,run_checks,config,checks}` on `design-`/`quality-discovery-agent` too; the enablement migration family (150, 188, 189, 190, 194, 215, **434**); and any handoff line reading "enable the N checks, config-only, no roll needed".
- **fires when:** you do the normal, correct thing — the check exists in the repo, you have read its `init()`, the migration is config-only so no image roll is needed, it applies with `UPDATE 1`, and `jsonb_array_length` goes up by exactly the number you added. Every signal you have says done. If the RUNNING pod predates the commit that registered the check, the name resolves to nothing at dispatch and the check never runs — for ever, silently, with no error row, no work items, and an array that reads correct in every query you would think to run.
- **the tell — there isn't one at the config layer, and that is the whole trap.** "Enabled and finding nothing" and "enabled and never executing" produce byte-identical evidence: the same array, the same absent work items. It is worse for a **self-gating** check (the directory family gates on a per-site opt-in flag AND on register data), because you *expect* zero findings, so the one observation that would expose the gap is the one you have already explained away. `215`'s header records the mechanism — an unregistered NAME is skipped, not an error — but a header on a different migration is not a check you will run.
- **the check:** ask the RUNNING BINARY for the name before you apply, and run **both controls in the same breath** (a bare probe that returns nothing is indistinguishable from a broken probe):
  ```
  POD=$(kubectl -n ai-persona-system get pods -l app=agent-chassis -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
  kubectl -n ai-persona-system exec $POD -- sh -c '
    grep -aq "<your_new_check_name>"            /proc/1/exe && echo new:PRESENT || echo new:ABSENT
    grep -aq "<a check you KNOW is enabled>"    /proc/1/exe && echo pos:PRESENT || echo pos:ABSENT
    grep -aq "missing_zzz_nonexistent_check_qqq" /proc/1/exe && echo neg:PRESENT || echo neg:ABSENT'
  ```
  Want `new:PRESENT pos:PRESENT neg:ABSENT`. `pos:ABSENT` or `neg:PRESENT` means the probe is broken and the run tells you nothing about the new name. **Never `strings`** (absent from the debian-slim images — behind the customary `2>/dev/null` its failure is indistinguishable from "not stamped") and never a discovery grep for "some check-shaped string". `[MEASURED 2026-08-16, migration 434, pod agent-chassis-584b6fcf-9mtqd: PRESENT / PRESENT / ABSENT.]` The durable version of the same question is the build stamp: `kubectl -n ai-persona-system logs -l app=<service> --tail=300 | grep -m1 'build provenance'`, then `git merge-base --is-ancestor <the commit that registered your check> <the stamp>`.
- **also state the expected SILENCE where the next reader will be:** if the check self-gates, write into the migration header and the handoff *why* zero findings is correct and *what event* first makes it speak (for 434: a site opting into a finance directory kind — the Phase C pilot). Otherwise the first person to look inherits a silence with two explanations and no way to choose.
- **relations:** LANDMINES "A census over `workflow.steps.*.action` is BLIND to every action nested in a `sub_workflow`" (same family: a well-formed answer that omits what you asked) · LANDMINES "the `checks` array you are reading may belong to `scan_sites_for_maintenance`, not `run_discovery_checks`" (the other half — filter to agents that actually HAVE the step; three do, not four) · `MEMORY/prove-a-deploy-at-the-artefact-index.md` · `MEMORY/a-post-fix-zero-needs-a-demand-control.md` (the same shape: a zero from a blind instrument) · CLAUDE.md "Ask the service what it is running. Do not hunt for markers, and do not use `strings`" · `194`/`215`/`434` headers
- **added:** 2026-08-16, portfolio_positioning lane (Phase B3f — probed before applying, which is why this is a check and not a WRONG_CALL)

### The tool generator's "already exists" probe ignores `build_status`, so a WITHDRAWN tool still counts as present — the rebuild run completes, writes nothing, and reports success

- **footprint:** `platform/orchestration/actions/create_tool_component_action.go` (the `--- Check if already exists ---` query, ~lines 197–227) · `content_components.is_active` for any row with `component_level='tool'` · re-filing an `add_tool` work item for a tool that has been built on this site before · `page_components.build_status='removed'` used as a tombstone for a tool slot
- **fires when:** you retry a tool build that went wrong. The first attempt left a component behind — a hollow fork, a bad reimplementation you withdrew, a deploy you rolled back by setting its placement `removed`. You do the careful thing: retire the placement rather than delete it (correct — it is the revert handle), then file the rebuild. The generator matches the OLD component, returns `{already_exists: true, component_id: <the dud>}`, and stops. The orchestration reaches `complete`, the work item completes with an empty `error`, no `agent_error_log` row is written, and **nothing whatsoever was built.**
- **the mechanism:** the probe joins `content_components → page_components → pages` on `cc.function`, `cc.component_level='tool'`, `p.site_id` and **`cc.is_active = true`, `LIMIT 1` — there is no predicate on `pc.build_status` at all.** So the join is satisfied by a placement in ANY state, `removed` and `pending` included. Retiring a placement is exactly the operation that is supposed to make a tool re-buildable, and it is the one thing that does not affect this query.
- **the tell — there is almost none, which is why it earns an entry.** A successful build and a no-op are the same `complete` status with the same empty error. The only distinguishing evidence is inside the run: `collected_data->'create_result'` holds `{already_exists:true, component_id, function}` and **lacks `page_adopted`, `page_id`, `generated` and `component_id` pointing at anything new**. A fast completion is a hint, not proof (a real adopt run took 54 s end to end, 2026-08-16).
- **the check:** before re-filing, ask whether a live component already claims the function — and deactivate it if the answer is a component you have withdrawn:
  ```sql
  SELECT cc.id, cc.is_active, pc.build_status AS placement
  FROM content_components cc
  JOIN page_components pc ON pc.component_id=cc.id
  JOIN pages p ON p.id=pc.page_id
  WHERE cc.function='<tool-function>' AND cc.component_level='tool'
    AND p.site_id='<site>' AND cc.is_active;          -- any row here ⇒ the generator will no-op
  UPDATE content_components SET is_active=false, updated_at=now()
  WHERE id='<the withdrawn component>' AND function='<tool-function>' AND is_active;   -- expect 1 row
  ```
  Then grade the RUN, not the item: `create_result.page_adopted` must be `true` and `create_result` must NOT contain `already_exists`. The `removed` placement row stays as history either way.
- **why not "just fix the query":** the probe is also the per-site uniqueness throttle that stops two sessions building the same tool twice, and `is_active` is a real signal — a component you intend to keep should block a rebuild. The defect is only that a withdrawn placement does not reach `is_active`. Deactivating the component is the intended expression of "I withdrew this"; the trap is that the tombstone everyone reaches for (`build_status='removed'`) is on the wrong table to be seen here.
- **relations:** `bugs_open/286` (the adopt-existing-page fix, live `v1.0.1304` — this probe sits immediately before the path 286 added) · register **TL-044** · LANDMINES "`deploy_image_asset` resolves its source image by PURPOSE, not by the `asset_id` you passed it" (same family: a resolver keyed on something coarser than the identity you supplied, returning `success:true`) · `MEMORY/a-complete-work-item-is-not-a-repaired-artefact.md` · `docs024_key_docs_latest/webdesign_tool_rebuilds/RUNBOOK_…` (the worked case: fork `cd60486c…`, `tool-ab-test-calculator`)
- **added:** 2026-08-16, `webdesign_tool_rebuilds` lane (read from source while scoping the batch, before it bit — the ab-test refile has not been attempted yet)

### A council submission whose edit names TWO files ("a/b.go + c/d.yaml") is refused server-side, spends ~30 minutes of queue, and records NO readable reason anywhere — it reads exactly like "still queued"

- **footprint:** `docs/agent_docs/docs024_key_docs_latest/fixloop_eg_dartsonline/097_TRIGGER_council_review_v1.sh` · `platform/orchestration/actions/diagnose_persist_fix_plan_action.go` (`editProblems`, `validateFixPlan`, `noOpEditReason`) · `0NN_council_gate.sql` step `persist_submission` · any `COUNCIL_SUBMISSION_*.json` · `orchestration_states.current_step='complete_invalid'`
- **fires when:** you write a submission edit that legitimately spans two files and name them in one `.file` field — a comment correction touching a source file and a config, say. It reads perfectly to a human, it satisfies **every one of the trigger script's client-side checks**, and the server refuses it. Same for a leading `/` or any `..`.
- **the tell — there is NO error message, and that is the trap.** The server's rule is `editProblems()`: `strings.ContainsAny(f, " \t\n")`, `strings.HasPrefix(f, "/")`, `strings.Contains(f, "..")` → *"file path must be repo-relative with no traversal or whitespace"*. But with `repair_step` unset (the council gate does not set one) the step just fails, and **measured 2026-08-16 on corr `85971036`: `diagnosis_artifacts` for that correlation → 0 rows of ANY kind; `collected_data` → nothing but `input_data`; `collected_data->>'__step_error'` → empty.** The only signal is `current_step='complete_invalid'` with `status='COMPLETED'` — and `COMPLETED` is the word that makes you stop looking. A missing verdict row is normally latency (CLAUDE.md says do not retry on that evidence), so the correct habit for the normal case is exactly what hides this one.
- **the check, BEFORE you submit** — `097` now runs it as its fifth trap (added 2026-08-16, this incident), but run it yourself on anything you hand-edited: `jq -r '.plan.edits[].file | select(test("[[:space:]]") or startswith("/") or contains(".."))' <submission.json>`. Any output at all = it will die server-side. **ONE EDIT = ONE FILE.** At the 8-edit cap, split the offender and MERGE two edits that touch the SAME file (two of mine were both `max_tokens_test.go`), rather than dropping content.
- **and check `current_step`, not just the verdict table, when a council run is "slow":** `SELECT current_step, status FROM orchestration_states WHERE collected_data->'input_data'->>'fix_correlation_id' = '<SUBMISSION_CORR>' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 1;` — `complete_invalid` = refused, no credits spent, **resubmit now**; `EXECUTING_STEP` = genuinely queued, wait. One query separates them and saves an hour of waiting for a verdict that is never coming.
- **⚠ the reason is DERIVABLE but not READABLE.** I got no error string back — none was recorded. What identified the cause was reading `editProblems` and then **re-implementing its exact predicate in Python and running it over my own submission**, which flagged precisely 2 of 8 edits (plan 19,093 bytes against a 65,536 cap; 8 edits against a cap of 8, so neither of the other plausible causes). If you hit this, do that rather than guessing: the validator's source is the only statement of the rule that exists.
- **source:** `bugs_open/257` lane, 2026-08-16 — first submission `85971036` died this way; corrected resubmission `366efae9`. The four earlier traps in `097` (operation allowlist, `grounded_in` must be strings, `risks` must be a string, comment-only sketch) were each added after the same class of silent server-side death; this is the fifth
- **added:** 2026-08-16, bugfix_257_token_budget_at_the_client lane

### Every session's scratchpad lives in ONE git repo — a `git restore .` typed from your scratch dir wipes ~40 other sessions' working files, and nothing warns you

- **footprint:** `/home/ant/.claude-scratch/claude-1000` (and any `.../<session-uuid>/scratchpad/...` path under it) · `git checkout` / `git restore` / `git clean` / `git reset --hard` run with the shell's cwd inside a scratchpad · `git archive HEAD | tar -x -C <scratchpad>` isolated-tree recipes
- **fires when:** you build an isolated copy of the repo in the scratchpad — the sanctioned way to test while other sessions hold the shared package uncompilable — and then run a git command "in the copy". The copy is NOT a repo (`git archive` extracts no `.git`), so git walks UP and finds the scratchpad root's repo instead. Nothing in the prompt says the scratchpad is versioned, and its per-session subdirectory makes it read as private space.
- **the trap:** `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` from any scratch subdirectory returns **`/home/ant/.claude-scratch/claude-1000`** — one repo holding **every** session's scratchpad. Measured 2026-08-16: **55 dirty files spanning ~40 session UUIDs** at one moment, including other lanes' council submissions, watcher scripts and census SQL. So a pathspec-less `git restore .` / `git checkout .` / `git clean -fd` there is the scratchpad equivalent of the `git stash` disaster CLAUDE.md bans — except **no hook blocks it**: `scripts/block-git-stash.py` covers `stash` only, and these commands are not stash.
- **the check, before any git command whose cwd might be under the scratchpad:** `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` first, and if it answers `.claude-scratch`, do not run a mutating git command at all — you have nothing there that needs versioning. `cd` to the project before running git, or use `git -C /home/ant/projects/agentchassis …` explicitly.
- **what is safe, and why it is a bad thing to rely on:** a BARE `git checkout` (no pathspec, no branch) only prints the modified-file list and takes no action — which is exactly how this was survived rather than paid for. The output looks alarming (55 `M` lines scrolling past, all other sessions' files) and is in fact the report, not the damage. Verify with `git -C $(git rev-parse --show-toplevel) status --porcelain | wc -l` — an unchanged count means nothing was reverted.
- **source:** 2026-08-16, `bugs_open/284` lane (`docs024_key_docs_latest/bugfix_284_flag_only_items_promoted/`), NOTES "near miss: the scratchpad root is a shared git repo"
- **added:** 2026-08-16, bugfix_284 lane

### A Go struct-literal census by FIELD VALUE (`grep 'HandlerAgent: ""'`) cannot see a producer that OMITS the field — and the omitted-field site is usually the one doing the most damage

- **footprint:** `platform/orchestration/actions/discovery_checks/` (`WorkItemSpec` literals: `HandlerAgent`, `Status`, `Severity`, `Priority`, `ItemKey`) · `platform/orchestration/actions/load_work_item_actions.go` (`workItem` struct literals) · any `grep -rn 'FieldName: *""'` used to enumerate producers
- **fires when:** you audit "which producers file X with an empty/zero Y" across a family of struct literals. Go zero-values every field the literal omits, so a site that simply never mentions `HandlerAgent` produces byte-identical rows to one that writes `HandlerAgent: ""` — and your grep returns a confident, complete-looking list that excludes it.
- **the trap, measured:** auditing `bugs_open/284`, `grep -rn -B12 'HandlerAgent: *"",'` over `platform/` + `internal/` returned **16 producer sites** and looked exhaustive. It missed `check_image_url_404.go` (three literals, field absent, comment says *"HandlerAgent intentionally empty — flag-only"*) — whose rows were **40 of the 60** in the class, more than twice the item_type the bug had been filed about. Scoping the fix from the grep would have fixed a third of the damage and closed the case.
- **the check:** ask the DATA which values exist, THEN find their producers — `SELECT item_type, status, count(*) FROM site_work_items WHERE handler_agent='' GROUP BY 1,2;` and grep for each `item_type` string. The DB knows about fields the source never mentions. If you must scan source, scan for the TYPE NAME (`WorkItemSpec{`) and inspect each literal's field SET, never for a field's value.
- **the same shape bites tests:** a test asserting "no producer sets an empty handler with a dispatchable status" by scanning source inherits exactly this blindness, which is why `bugs_open/284`'s guard was put in the promoter's SQL rather than in a source-scanning test.
- **source:** 2026-08-16, `bugs_open/284` lane; NOTES "the class is bigger than the type 284 named"; WRONG_CALLS 2026-08-16
- **added:** 2026-08-16, bugfix_284 lane

## The producer's status literal you are reading today may have been changed BY THE VERY FIX you are evaluating — so "the code files `deferred`, therefore a `detected`-only mechanism can't have touched these rows" is not a refutation

- **footprint:** `platform/orchestration/actions/discovery_checks/check_*.go` (`Status:` / `HandlerAgent:` literals in `WorkItemSpec`) · `site_work_items.status` · any repair or diagnosis that reasons from a producer's CURRENT source to rows filed WEEKS ago · `bugs_closed/284`
- **the trap:** reading `check_palette_contrast.go` and `check_content_duplication.go` at HEAD on 2026-08-17 shows `capability_gap` filed with `Status: "deferred"`. The promoter that stamped 18 such rows `blocked` only ever touched `detected`. That reads as a clean refutation of the whole diagnosis — and it is wrong: **`deferred` was introduced by 284's OWN fix commit `7027a2801`**, in the same change as the promoter guard. The rows really were born `detected`, under the pre-fix code. A council-approved diagnosis, a repair of 60 rows and a CHECK constraint all sat on the "refuted" premise; abandoning it on that reading would have left the rows misdescribed and the door open.
- **why it is invisible:** nothing in the file says when the literal changed, and a fix that repairs a producer AND a consumer in one commit is normal, good practice — so the strongest evidence for the bug (the fix) is also what erases the bug's fingerprints from the source. The rows' own timeline is the surviving witness.
- **the check, one command before you believe any such refutation:** `git log --format='%h %ad %s' --date=short -S'Status:    "deferred"' -- <the check file>` — if it names the fix commit, the present-day literal post-dates the rows and says nothing about how they were filed. Pair it with the rows' own dates: `SELECT min(created_at)::date, max(created_at)::date, max(updated_at)::date FROM site_work_items WHERE <the population>` — 284's 18 rows were all filed 07-28..08-10 and blocked 08-02..08-11, **none since**, which is the shape of a mechanism that has already been closed rather than one that never existed.
- **generalises past status literals:** any `HandlerAgent`, `ItemType`, `Priority` or default that a fix normalises. The question to ask is never "what does the producer do?" but "what did it do WHEN THESE ROWS WERE WRITTEN?".
- **source:** 2026-08-17, `bugs_closed/284` repair session, caught before the repair by checking a contradiction rather than accepting it. Related: MEMORY [[a-closed-bugs-scope-out-expires]] (a premise decays) and [[seed-sql-is-history-live-row-is-fact]] (the same asymmetry between code and the state it produced).
- **relations:** `bugs_closed/284` · `bugs_closed/279` · migration `442` (the repair, whose header carries this warning inline)
- **added:** 2026-08-17, bugs_closed/284 repair session

### A fabricated needle made of ZEROS is present in every binary — the must-be-absent control that cannot fail

- **footprint:** `kubectl exec … grep -a "<needle>" /proc/1/exe` · any build-provenance or literal probe · `deployed_image_read_audit.go` · the "always run a control in the same breath" rule
- **fires when:** you do the right thing — pair a must-be-PRESENT probe with a must-be-ABSENT one — and reach for an obviously-fake needle like `0000000000000000000000000000000000000000` or `aaaa…`. **It comes back PRESENT.** Long zero runs occur naturally in a binary's zero-filled data, and a repeated-character string is exactly what a padded region looks like.
- **why the wrong result looks exactly like the right one:** it does not fail silently — it fails *loudly and misleadingly*. The control reports "this grep matches everything", so the correct reading of a sound measurement gets thrown away as unreliable. Measured 2026-08-17 probing chassis `v1.0.1305`: the zeros control read PRESENT while the stamp probe was in fact perfectly discriminating — two **real** commit shas that were not the stamp both read ABSENT in the same exec.
- **the check:** make the negative control **fabricated but PLAUSIBLE** — a real commit sha that is not the one you expect, or the pre-fix spelling of the very string your change replaced (which is the strongest form: it proves the binary is post-fix, not merely that a word is in it). Never a constant-character run, never a value whose bytes could occur as padding.
- **relation:** this sharpens the standing entry against a *discovery* grep for "some 40-hex string" (which matches Go's internal digit table). Same family, opposite direction: that one makes an absent thing look present by searching too loosely; this one makes a sound probe look broken by choosing a needle that was never absent.
- **source:** 2026-08-17, `bugfix_265_legacy_dialect_unrepresentable` lane, verifying v1.0.1305
- **added:** 2026-08-17, bugfix_265 lane


### `failed` work items carry NO `completed_at` — so any pair-health or success-rate query keyed on that column reports 100% success for everything, and cannot come out otherwise

- **footprint:** `site_work_items.completed_at` · `site_work_items.status` · `idx_swi_completed` · any "how often does this handler actually work?" / success-ratio / pair-health query · `scheduled_tasks.detected-item-promoter` pre_query · migrations `430`, `444`
- **fires when:** you measure a handler's or an `(item_type, handler_agent)` pair's track record and reach for `completed_at` as the "when did this finish" column — the natural choice, and the one the index name endorses. `idx_swi_completed` is defined `btree (completed_at) WHERE status IN ('complete','verified','rejected','wont_fix')` — **`failed` is not in that list**, and the column is only written on the success path.
- **the trap, measured 2026-08-17:** `SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE status='failed') … WHERE completed_at < <t>` returned **0 failures for every pair**, so a counterfactual computing each pair's health at the moment it was promoted reported **100% success across all 17 pairs** — including `literal_markdown -> page-build-handler`, whose real record at that instant was **1 complete against 28 failed (3%)**. The wrong answer is not empty or malformed; it is a clean, plausible, uniformly-excellent table, which is exactly what you hope to see and therefore do not question.
- **the control that catches it in one line:** `SELECT status, count(*), count(completed_at) FROM site_work_items WHERE status IN ('failed','complete') GROUP BY 1;` → **failed 265 rows / 0 with completed_at**, complete 5921 / 5882. If the two arms do not differ, your time filter is not measuring what you think.
- **the check:** key terminal-history queries on **`updated_at`** (every terminal write bumps it, via `trg_site_work_items_updated_at`) and filter on `status` alone for the counting. And whenever a ratio comes back at or near 100% for *every* group, treat the uniformity itself as the symptom — a healthy population has a spread.
- **relation:** the same family as MEMORY's *"your measurement answers the question you ENCODED"* — here the encoding silently drops one entire arm of the comparison, so the disconfirming result was unreachable. Compare the "a filtered count can ship inside a DENOMINATOR" case; this is the numerator's twin.
- **source:** 2026-08-17, `bugfix_277_required_fields_repair` lane, writing migration `444`'s success-floor door-closer. Caught because the all-100% table was implausible, not because the query looked wrong. WRONG_CALLS 2026-08-17.
- **added:** 2026-08-17, bugfix_277/083 lane

### The per-slot TEXT floor counts CSS and JAVASCRIPT as text — so a write that deletes every word of prose and adds a stylesheet reads as GROWTH and is allowed, and the one thing it does refuse is a repair

- **footprint:** `platform/orchestration/actions/save_sections_shrink_guard.go` (`shrinkGuardTagStripper`, `evaluateSectionShrink`, `minShrinkGuardChars`) · `single_slot_floors.go` · `save_page_sections` / `apply_section_edit` (`content_edit`) · any claim of the form "the floors would have caught it" · `section_shrink_floor` step config
- **fires when:** you reason about, or rely on, the text shrink floor while looking at a slot that carries an inline `<style>` or `<script>` block — every ported page, every tool slot, most guide pages. The floor's axis is `<[^>]*>`-stripped length: it removes TAGS but not what is INSIDE style/script, so a replacement that drops the entire article body while adding a wrapper stylesheet MEASURES BIGGER.
- **the numbers, on the real pair that caused it** (`bugs_closed/285`, `page_component_history ab400131…` vs the poison row, measured 2026-08-17 through `datahelpers.VisibleTextFromHTML`): tag-stripped 3,236 → 8,491 = **262% "kept"** (floor 50%, so allowed); class attributes 3 → 4 = **133%** (the sibling floor, also allowed); VISIBLE text 2,143 → **16** = **0.7%**. The page served an empty `<article>` plus three fabricated download links for ~23 hours, and every guard on the path reported no violation.
- **and the direction nobody expects:** across all 117 archived overwrite pairs the tag-stripped axis fires exactly ONCE, on the **repair** — putting the article back reads 38% on that axis (16 → 2,143 on the visible one). So the axis you might reach for as a safety net is, on eight days of real history, a net that catches only the fix. The visible axis fires three times, and the other two are **tool slots hollowed to 0 visible characters while their tag-stripped length GREW** (`idea.uk/tool-ab-test-calculator` 684 → 0 with 10,399 → 12,929 tag-stripped, 2026-08-11; the same tool on webdesign.co.uk, 2026-08-15 — `bugs_open/286`). The two axes agree on **zero** pairs in eight days.
- **the check:** never measure section content with a tag-strip alone. In Go use `datahelpers.VisibleTextFromHTML` (a real parsed walk excluding script/style/noscript/template/code/pre/svg/iframe/textarea/select/option/head, entities decoded) — `visibleTextLength` in `section_visible_text.go` is just a non-whitespace count over it; in SQL the same thing is `regexp_replace(regexp_replace(regexp_replace(h,'<style[^>]*>.*?</style>','','gis'),'<script[^>]*>.*?</script>','','gis'),'<[^>]+>','','g')`. The SQL is an APPROXIMATION of the Go measure (it keeps `<code>`/`<pre>` text and does not decode entities), so use it for censuses and the Go helper for decisions. Pair any "did this edit lose content?" query with BOTH axes and expect them to disagree on exactly these slots. **Live status:** the section-editor call site measures visible text (council `3279156b`); the WHOLE-PAGE path still measures tag-stripped length, because its DELETE+INSERT writes cannot be paired from the archive — `bugs_open/293` holds the evidence gap and two ways to close it. So which axis guards a given write depends on which writer ran.
- **relations:** `bugs_closed/285` (the incident) · `bugs_open/293` (the unfixed half) · `bugs_open/178` (the floor) / `bugs_open/253` (the class floor and the council round that wired both into the editor) · `bugs_open/286` + the LANDMINE "A `section_edit` on a per-site TOOL FORK whose template carries `{{.field}}` copy…" (the same missing axis found from the tool-fork end, by the webdesign_tool_rebuilds lane) · MEMORY [[a-complete-work-item-is-not-a-repaired-artefact]]
- **⚠ figures CORRECTED in place, same day (2026-08-17):** the first version of this entry quoted 2,754 → 68 visible chars and "the visible axis refuses exactly one pair". Those came from a SQL-regex approximation; the shipped implementation delegates to `datahelpers.VisibleTextFromHTML` (a real parsed walk), and re-running all 117 pairs through it gives 2,143 → 16 and THREE refusals. Same verdict, different numbers — recorded because a reader who saw the earlier figures should know which set the code actually produces.
- **added:** 2026-08-17, bugfix_285_shared_template_write lane

### The binary stamps exactly ONE sha — the build HEAD — so grepping YOUR commit's sha in `/proc/1/exe` returns 0 even when your change is definitely in the image

- **footprint:** `/proc/1/exe` · `grep -acF <sha>` against any backend pod · `kubectl exec … -- grep -a` build-provenance probes · "did my fix ship?" · `make build-<service>` / `IMAGE_TAG` · `git merge-base --is-ancestor` · CLAUDE.md "Building & deploying images"
- **fires when:** you take CLAUDE.md's advice to prove a deploy at the artefact, the startup `build provenance` log line has already scrolled out of reach (it does within hours on a busy service), so you fall back to the binary probe — and you grep for **your own commit's sha**. It returns `0`. The natural reading is "my fix did not ship", and it is wrong: only the commit the image was BUILT from is stamped. Every ancestor commit — including yours, whose code is compiled into the very binary you are grepping — is absent as a literal.
- **the mechanism, measured 2026-08-17** on `agent-chassis-5657f446c7-q7b82` (image `v1.0.1305`, pod started 2026-08-16 22:07Z): commit `7a276dc9c9433d159bfffcdc59d0675c8fb7fad5`, dated 2026-08-15 and confirmed an ancestor of HEAD by `git merge-base --is-ancestor`, so its code is unquestionably in that image — `grep -acF` for it in `/proc/1/exe` returns **0**. **Positive control in the same probe:** `grep -acF "build provenance"` returns **1**, so the probe itself works and the zero is about the sha, not the method. A sha is a 40-char literal that appears in the binary only if the build stamped it; being an ancestor puts your *code* in, never your *identifier*.
- **the tell — there isn't one, which is the point.** `0` and `1` are both well-formed answers and the command exits cleanly either way. Note `grep -acF` also **exits 1 on no match**, so a probe written with `&&` or behind the customary `2>/dev/null` silently reports nothing at all.
- **the check:** never ask "is my sha in the binary?". Ask **"which sha did this build come from?"**, then answer your real question with git.
  > **UPDATED 2026-08-17 (same day, same lane): ASK THE IMAGE'S LABEL FIRST — it is one command and there is nothing to guess.** `docker inspect aqls/<svc>@sha256:<the imageID from kubectl> --format '{{index .Config.Labels "org.opencontainers.image.revision"}}'` returns the build commit outright, and works on the RUNNING image addressed by digest. The candidate-probing recipe below is the FALLBACK for when the image is not locally addressable — it is not the first move, and I wrote it as though it were. See the same-tag-rebuild entry above for the worked pair.
  Fallback: find the build HEAD by probing candidate commits with `grep -acF` (walk back from the tip nearest the pod's start time until one returns 1), or read the startup line if it is still in range — `kubectl -n ai-persona-system logs -l app=<service> --tail=300 | grep -m1 'build provenance'`. Then: `git merge-base --is-ancestor <your-commit> <the build sha>` — exit 0 means your change shipped. **Always run a two-sided control in the same breath**: one literal that must be present (`build provenance`) and one sha that must be absent, or you cannot distinguish "not stamped" from "probe broken". Per SERVICE, never per fleet (`bugs_open/249`).
- **relations:** LANDMINES "a criteria check type the running browser-runner binary does not know is SKIPPED" (the sibling trap — short Go string literals compile to immediate comparisons and never reach rodata, so a short marker also greps 0 on a binary that fully supports it; together they mean **no `grep -c` of a short literal is evidence either way**) · CLAUDE.md "Building & deploying images" (which already says ask the binary, not git — this entry is why the *naive* way of asking returns the wrong answer) · `MEMORY/prove-a-deploy-at-the-artefact-index.md`
- **source:** flagged as a candidate by the `bugfix_281_tool_audit_ported` lane 2026-08-16; **written and verified first-hand 2026-08-17** by the session that took its handoff forward (the probe and both controls above are that verification, not a relay).
- **added:** 2026-08-17, `bugfix_281_tool_audit_ported` lane

### A stalled `audit_tool` item costs THREE Sonnet audits, not an unbounded retry — and the "every ~40 minutes" figure in the 281 handoff is a single item generalised

- **footprint:** `site_work_items` where `item_type='audit_tool'` · the claimed-item-timeout sweep · `orchestration_states` grouped by `collected_data->'input_data'->>'work_item_id'` · `tool-auditor` · any cost estimate for a stalled handler item
- **fires when:** you cost a stall. A `tool-auditor` run that never completes leaves its item claimed, the claimed-item-timeout sweep releases and re-dispatches it, and each re-dispatch pays for a **fresh Sonnet audit of the whole tool**. The trap is the *size* of that bill: the `bugfix_281` handoff recorded "a fresh Sonnet audit each ~40 min until `failed`", which reads as an unbounded loop and would justify emergency action.
- **the correction, measured 2026-08-17** across every `audit_tool` item with more than one orchestration: the per-item orchestration count **caps at 3** — 3 is the maximum anywhere in the table, not a sample — and the mean gap between attempts is **43, 59, 128, 129, 147, 147 minutes**. So the true cost is **≤3 audits over roughly 1–5 hours, then the item goes `failed`**. The single item that does show ~43 min (`1bfd5d1e-…`) is the 281 lane's OWN hand-filed probe, which is where the figure came from; generalising one item's cadence to the class overstated the rate by ~3x and the total by an unbounded factor.
- **the tell:** a rate quoted without the cap. "Every N minutes until X" is a claim about *two* numbers — the interval and the terminating condition — and the terminating condition is the one that decides whether the bill is bounded. If a doc gives you the interval and not the count, get the count before you act on it.
- **the check:** one query, and it answers both halves at once —
  ```sql
  SELECT collected_data->'input_data'->>'work_item_id' AS item, count(*) AS attempts,
         round(EXTRACT(epoch FROM (max(created_at)-min(created_at)))/60
               /GREATEST(count(*)-1,1)) AS avg_gap_min
  FROM orchestration_states
  WHERE owner_agent_type='<handler>' AND collected_data->'input_data'->>'work_item_id' IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*) > 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 10;
  ```
  Read the **top** `attempts` value as the cap, and never take the gap from one row.
- **relations:** `bugs_open/289` (the defect that stalls these runs — fixed `509e01e6a`, inert until the roll) · `bugs_open/294` (why the stalled orchestrations were then immortal) · `WRONG_CALLS.md` 2026-08-16 "a commit message is an argument, not an API" (same failure: a relayed figure adopted without re-measuring — this entry exists because the relay was checked)
- **source:** candidate flagged by the `bugfix_281_tool_audit_ported` lane 2026-08-16 with the ~40 min figure; **measured and corrected 2026-08-17** by the session that took its handoff forward.
- **added:** 2026-08-17, `bugfix_281_tool_audit_ported` lane

### A `banned_claims` pattern seeded through dollar-quoted JSON is DOUBLE-ESCAPED, compiles cleanly, and matches nothing for ever — and the `jsonb_array_length(...) = N` check you wrote to prove it landed passes either way

- **footprint:** `platform/orchestration/datahelpers/claims.go`, `docs/agent_docs/docs024_key_docs_latest/portfolio_positioning/`, `banned_claims`, `ScanBannedClaims`, `evidence_base`
- **also fires on** (prose, not footprints — these cannot be grep keys): any `SEED_*.sql` writing `site_specs.aspect='evidence_base'`, and any dollar-quoted `$tag$ … $tag$` **JSON** literal holding a regex or a `\uXXXX` escape.
- **fires when:** you seed a site's claims guard and verify it the obvious way — count the patterns, see the number you expected, move on. Two escaping layers are in play and only one is visible: the dollar-quoted SQL string passes bytes **literally**, and the JSON parser **then** unescapes. So `\\\\b` in the file stores `\\b` (a literal backslash then `b`), and `\\u00a3` stores the six characters `£` instead of `£`.
- **why the wrong result looks exactly like the right one:** `claims.go` compiles with `regexp.Compile("(?i)"+p)` and falls back to `regexp.QuoteMeta` **only when compilation ERRORS**. `\\bguaranteed …` is a perfectly valid regex — it just never matches English prose — so it compiles, **the fallback never fires**, and the guard is loaded, listed, counted and inert. There is no error, no log line and no failure row; the site simply has no claims guard. **A pattern that fails to compile is caught. A pattern that compiles WRONG is not.**
- **`[MEASURED 2026-08-17, remortgagecalculator.uk pilot seed]`:** all **6 of 6** patterns inert on the first apply. The seed's own verify block asserted `jsonb_array_length(banned_claims) = 6` and **passed** — a count comes out identical whether the guards work or not, which is the same shape as `WRONG_CALLS`' "a `[MEASURED]` figure is only evidence if it could have come out otherwise".
- **the check — probe, never count.** Assert BEHAVIOUR with strings that must match *and* strings that must not (a guard matching everything is as broken as one matching nothing, and only the pair tells them apart). **Do it in Go, not SQL:** Postgres ARE and Go RE2 disagree on word boundaries — PG spells it `\y`, and `\b` is *backspace* — so a `psql … ~ pattern` probe is a check in the wrong engine and will lie to you in both directions. Worked pair: `datahelpers/claims_banned_pattern_escaping_test.go` (semantics, compiled exactly as production does) + the seed's own structural guard.
- **for the structural half, avoid `LIKE` entirely — use `position()` + `chr(92)`.** In `LIKE`, backslash is itself the default ESCAPE character, so `'%\b%'` means *"the letter b"* and would pass on any pattern containing `b`; `position(chr(92)||'b' in p) > 0` has no escape semantics to reason about. `chr(92)` also survives an authoring channel that rewrites `\uXXXX` into the character it denotes — which is how the same file's `£` check ended up searching for `£`, the very thing it was meant to confirm, and refusing correct data twice (MEMORY: `escape-sequence-emission-trap`).
- **prove the guard can fail before you trust it:** run the new structural check against the **still-broken** rows and require it to flag them (it reported 6 bad / 6 total), then against the fixed rows and require zero. A guard only validated on good data is untested.
- **relations:** `MEMORY/mutate-the-code-to-prove-the-guard.md` · `MEMORY/a-pass-from-a-blind-check-outlives-the-blindness.md` · LANDMINES "Adding a template variable to a prompt WITHOUT adding its field to that step's `input_fields` renders EMPTY and errors nothing" (same family: applied, silent, and structurally verifiable while functionally dead) · `bugs_open/012` (a rewrite that reports success having persisted a fragment) · `portfolio_positioning/SEED_2026-08-17b_remortgagecalculator_uk_fix_banned_claim_escaping.sql` (the correction, with the mechanism in its header)
- **added:** 2026-08-17, portfolio_positioning lane (found on its own Phase C pilot seed, minutes after applying it — by probing rather than counting)

### The whole build pipeline stops dispatching and NOTHING says so — items stay `triaged` with `attempt_count 0`, the dispatch loop COMPLETES every ~90s, and the reason is one row in `ai_endpoint_health`

- **footprint:** `ai_endpoint_health` · `platform/orchestration/actions/claim_work_item_action.go` (`extractAIEndpointFromHandler`, the health gate at ~line 218) · `build-dispatch-loop` · `build-pipeline-trigger` · `site_work_items.status='triaged'` · `scheduled_tasks` `ai-endpoint-health-check` · any hand-raised work item (`tool_acceptance_run.sh`, `090`/`097` triggers, `improve_tool`, `add_tool`)
- **fires when:** you raise a work item at the fleet and follow it. Every published symptom says "working": the item exists, `build-pipeline-trigger` fires on its 30s tick, `build-dispatch-loop` runs and reaches `status=COMPLETED`, its `pending.item_count` is 1 with `rows_dropped: 0`, and there is **no `__step_error` anywhere**. Your item simply never leaves `triaged`, and `attempt_count` stays 0 — so even the retry counter tells you nothing happened.
- **the mechanism:** `claim_work_item` looks up the handler agent's AI endpoint and reads `SELECT healthy FROM ai_endpoint_health WHERE endpoint_url = $1`. If the row says false it **releases the claim and sets the item back to `triaged`**. That is correct, deliberate behaviour — the work resumes when the endpoint recovers, nothing is lost — but it is invisible at every level a session normally looks. Note the asymmetry that makes it worse: **no row at all is treated as healthy** (a deliberate choice, commented in the code), so absence and health look the same and only the false row bites.
- **the second-order trap: one stuck item monopolises the dispatcher fleet-wide.** `build-pipeline-trigger`'s `find_dispatchable_site` is `ORDER BY wi.created_at ASC, wi.priority ASC, wi.id ASC LIMIT 1` — **one site per tick, strictly oldest item first**. An item that can be selected but never claimed is re-selected every cycle for ever, so every other site starves. Measured 2026-08-17: `webdesign.co.uk` took **18 of 18** dispatch-loop runs in one hour while two other sites' items sat untouched; over the preceding day the same site took **95** runs. Do not read "my site never gets a run" as a rotation problem — read the oldest triaged item in the fleet.
- **the check, and it is one query — read the CLAIM, not the item:**
  ```sql
  SELECT collected_data->'claim_result' FROM orchestration_states
   WHERE owner_agent_type='build-dispatch-loop' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 1;
  -- {"claimed": false, "reason": "ai_endpoint_unavailable", "endpoint": "https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages"}
  SELECT endpoint_url, healthy, last_healthy, error FROM ai_endpoint_health;
  ```
  `execution_path` is `[]` on these runs, so use `collected_data`'s keys instead: `process_item_iter_0_check_claim` present with no `spawn_handler` IS the signature.
- **⚠ and the reason may not be a fault at all — it may be a spend cap.** Hit live 2026-08-17 11:08Z: `healthy=f`, error `API request failed with status 400 … "You have reached your specified API usage limits. You will regain access on 2026-09-01 at 00:00 UTC."` That is an **account limit set in the provider console, not an outage**, so no amount of waiting, retrying or re-dispatching helps and the health check (hourly) will keep confirming it. 26 items were blocked within the hour. **Read the `error` column before diagnosing anything**, and confirm against a second source — `SELECT created_at, agent_type, error_message FROM llm_call_log WHERE provider='anthropic' AND NOT success ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 5` — because a health table is an instrument and this entry is exactly the situation where a believable outage story invites you to trust it unchecked.
- **source:** 2026-08-17, leopardess lane, while following a hand-raised `acceptance_run` that never got claimed; the endpoint cap was found four queries later and explained three sites' stalled items at once
- **relations:** MEMORY [[detection-works-schedule-and-dispatch-do-not]] · [[a-plausible-external-cause-is-when-to-doubt-your-instrument]] · [[a-complete-work-item-is-not-a-repaired-artefact]] · LANDMINES "Enabling a `scheduled_tasks` row proves nothing" (the sibling shape: the task fires and dispatches nothing)
- **added:** 2026-08-17, leopardess voice/acceptance lane

> **⚠ CORRECTED 2026-08-17 12:55 BST (11:55Z) by the loanandmortgagecalculator lane, ~50 minutes
> after the entry above was written.** The entry is right that the 400 is an account limit rather
> than an outage, and right that `ai_endpoint_health` must be read for its `error` column. **Its
> practical conclusion — "no amount of waiting, retrying or re-dispatching helps" until
> 2026-09-01 — did not hold, and a session that believes it will not dispatch anything for two
> weeks.** Measured just now, `[MEASURED 2026-08-17 11:55Z]`:
>
> ```sql
> SELECT provider, success, count(*), max(created_at) FROM llm_call_log
>  WHERE created_at > now() - interval '90 minutes' GROUP BY 1,2;
> --  anthropic | f |  4 | 2026-08-17 11:09:53Z
> --  anthropic | t | 97 | 2026-08-17 11:54:39Z   <-- 23 seconds before the query
> SELECT count(*), count(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT success) FROM llm_call_log
>  WHERE created_at > now() - interval '20 minutes';   -- 28 calls, 0 failures
> ```
>
> So live `provider='anthropic'` traffic recovered within minutes and is healthy now, while
> `ai_endpoint_health` **still reads `healthy=f` with `last_healthy = 11:07:15Z`** and the
> September message in `error`. The limit was window-scoped in practice; the row is not tracking
> the recovery, because nothing has re-probed it successfully since.
>
> **So the check inverts: `ai_endpoint_health` is the instrument and `llm_call_log` is the
> traffic.** Read the health row for *why* something failed at a moment in the past; read the
> call log to answer "can I dispatch now?". A red health row with a fresh successful call log
> means the row is stale, not that the fleet is down — which is the same lesson the entry itself
> draws one line earlier about believable outage stories, applied to its own conclusion.
> `[UNMEASURED]` whether the 4 failures and the 97 successes share one key/limit bucket; the
> dispatchable-now answer does not depend on it.

## The BUILD QUEUE can be fully stopped while every liveness check says the fleet is healthy — `claim_work_item` gates on `ai_endpoint_health`, and that row is re-probed ONCE AN HOUR

- **footprint:** `ai_endpoint_health` (the `claude` row, `check_interval_seconds`) · `platform/orchestration/actions/claim_work_item_action.go` (the "AI endpoint health check" block, `reason: ai_endpoint_unavailable`) · `check_endpoint_health_action.go` (the prober, `claude_ping`) · `build-dispatch-loop` (`load_items`/`process_item`) · `build-pipeline-trigger` (`find_dispatchable_site`) · any question of the form "why has my work item not dispatched?"
- **fires when:** you create a work item, see the dispatch loop running on schedule, confirm the loop LOADS your item, and confirm LLM calls are succeeding fleet-wide — and conclude the queue is merely slow. It is stopped. One 400 from the AI endpoint (an intermittent usage cap: `bugs_open/243`) flips `ai_endpoint_health.healthy` to false; `claim_work_item` then RELEASES every claim fleet-wide and sets the item back to `triaged`; and because `find_dispatchable_site` is `ORDER BY created_at ASC … LIMIT 1` across ALL sites, the whole fleet queues behind one item that can never clear. The row is re-probed on `check_interval_seconds` = **3600**, so the stop outlives the outage by up to an hour
- **the tell — and why the obvious checks all read GREEN:** the dispatch loop runs to COMPLETION every ~90s (not stuck, not erroring); `pending.has_items = true` with your item in it; `orchestration_states` shows healthy completed runs; and `llm_call_log` shows real successes THROUGHOUT (measured 2026-08-17: 93 of 99 calls OK, latest 11:52:32Z, while zero items had been claimed since 10:32:33Z). **`SELECT max(created_at) FROM llm_call_log WHERE success` — the fleet's own recommended liveness query — reports UP while nothing can be claimed.** The only honest tell is in the loop's own `collected_data`: the path runs `claim → check_claim → done`, `spawn_handler` is never reached, and `claim_result` reads `{"claimed": false, "reason": "ai_endpoint_unavailable"}`
- **the check, before diagnosing any "my item won't dispatch":**
  ```sql
  SELECT healthy, last_checked, last_healthy, check_interval_seconds, left(error,120)
    FROM ai_endpoint_health WHERE name = 'claude';
  SELECT max(claimed_at) FROM site_work_items WHERE claimed_by = 'build-dispatch-loop';
  ```
  `healthy=f` plus no claim since about `last_checked` IS this, and no amount of waiting on your own item will show it. Read the claim result rather than the loop's status: a loop that claims nothing COMPLETES successfully. **Do not infer dispatch health from LLM health** — they are independent, and under an intermittent cap they disagree for an hour at a time
- **source:** 2026-08-17, webdesign_uk_build_service lane — found because it blocked a `bugs_open/285` acceptance run; full mechanism, timings and the three fix shapes in the 2026-08-17 addendum to `bugs_open/243`. The prober samples ONE call on `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` while live traffic is sonnet/opus, and `llm_call_log` holds zero haiku rows in 24h — so the probe's own model is cross-checkable from nothing
- **relations:** `bugs_open/243` (the cap this is downstream of) · `bugs_open/244` (the spend that triggers the cap) · LANDMINES "A stopped queue provokes exactly the kind of activity that makes the aggregate look alive" (the sibling shape, one level up) · MEMORY [[a-plausible-external-cause-is-when-to-doubt-your-instrument]]
- **added:** 2026-08-17, webdesign_uk_build_service lane

## A parked `field_updates` payload is a FULL-FIELD REPLACEMENT frozen at the moment it was computed — applying it later silently reverts every change made to that field since, and both the item and the apply report success

- **footprint:** `platform/orchestration/actions/section_editor_actions.go` (`applyContentEdit`, the `for k, v := range updates` merge at :746-748) · `apply_section_edit` · `site_work_items` rows whose `spec` carries `field_updates` (`section_edit`, `content_edit`, `copy_edit_proposed`) · `checkpoint_for_review` (`on_approve`) · any item parked at `needs_human_review` holding a proposed edit · `copy_quality_two_stage/gate_stage2_edit.py`
- **fires when:** you approve or hand-apply an edit that was proposed earlier — an hour, a day or a fortnight earlier — because a human had to look at it first. **The merge is per-FIELD, not per-change**: every field the payload NAMES is overwritten wholesale with the value captured when the proposal was written. If anything rewrote that field in between (a rerender, an improvement sweep, another lane's `content_rewrite`, a regeneration off a corrected plan), the apply throws it away and restores the older text. Nothing errors: `apply_section_edit` reports success, `content_edit_mode: field_updates`, `updated_field_count: 1`, the item completes, the page renders and deploys. **The reverted copy is well-formed and plausible, which is why nobody notices.**
- **why the review queue makes this the DEFAULT case, not an edge case:** the whole point of `checkpoint_for_review` is that time passes between proposing and applying, and `bugs_open/033` means that time is unbounded — 735 items sit at `needs_human_review`, the oldest from 2026-03-15. An estate that reviews before applying is an estate whose payloads go stale by design.
- **worse on a single-field component, which is common:** where a component declares ONE field (e.g. `ported-prose` declares only `content`), "the fields being edited" IS the whole component, so a stale payload reverts everything — headings, links, markup and all. The blast-radius argument for preferring `field_updates` over `replacement_content_data` (PLAN §9) buys exactly nothing there, and PLAN §10 already withdrew the stronger claim.
- **the check, before applying ANY parked edit:** re-grade against the CURRENT row, never against the payload's own record of what it edited. The proposal's stored "before" is the trap — it will agree with itself for ever.
  ```sql
  -- did the field move after the proposal was written?
  SELECT pc.updated_at AS component_changed_at, swi.created_at AS proposal_written_at,
         pc.updated_at > swi.created_at AS PAYLOAD_IS_STALE
    FROM site_work_items swi
    JOIN page_components pc ON pc.id = (swi.spec->>'page_component_id')::uuid
   WHERE swi.id = '<item>';
  ```
  A `t` in the last column means re-run the proposer, not the applier. `gate_stage2_edit.py --item <id>` does this the honest way round — it loads the component's live `content_data` as the "before", so a stale payload shows up as dropped links, lost classes or vanished figures rather than as a clean pass.
- **do NOT reach for `stop_reason` when checking whether the proposing call was truncated** — `llm_call_log` has no such column. Compare `output_tokens` against the step's configured `max_tokens`; equality means the completion was CUT and the payload may be a fragment that will still apply cleanly.
- **AND THE ADDRESS GOES STALE TOO, not just the content (added 2026-08-18, same lane).** A rerender does not update the component row — it **replaces** it with a new `id`. The proof case's `page_component_id` `d6c9198b…` was gone within a day, replaced by `f05d59e5…` at 09:55:37Z with `created_at = updated_at` (the content came through intact). So a parked proposal can hold a **dangling** `page_component_id`, and a tool that resolves it reports `no page_component <id>` — which reads like a typo or a bad copy-paste, not like "a rerender happened here". Resolve a parked edit by **(page_name, slot_name)** and treat the stored id as a hint: 016b §9's rule, arriving from the proposal side rather than the repair side. `CQ-023`'s classifier already keys this way and says why; anything that stores an id for later must expect it to die.
- **source:** 2026-08-17, `copy_quality_two_stage` — found while writing the apply instructions for stage 2's first proposal (`copy_edit_proposed` item `6dce90f1`, computed against a component that had been byte-stable for five days, which is what made the risk visible rather than what made it real). Register `CQ-024`; the re-grade step is step 1 of that lane's `HANDOFF_2026-08-17`.
- **relations:** `bugs_open/033` (the queue that makes payloads old) · `bugs_open/260` (the retype hazard on the same merge) · `bugs_open/238` (save REPLACES / rerender MERGES — the sibling shape one level up) · MEMORY [[a-stale-page-holds-every-improvement-since-it-rendered]] · MEMORY [[a-complete-work-item-is-not-a-repaired-artefact]]
- **added:** 2026-08-17, copy_quality_two_stage lane

### `create_work_item` with no `status` key births the row at 'triaged' — an item whose TYPE says needs_human_review still DISPATCHES
- **footprint:** `platform/orchestration/actions/create_work_item_action.go` (`status` default), any `agent_definitions` step whose `action` is `create_work_item`, `site_work_items.status`, `handler_agent`
- **fires when:** you write or copy a `create_work_item` step config for a parked/human-facing item and set `item_type` to a state-sounding word (`needs_human_review`) without an explicit `"status"` key — or you name a `handler_agent` you have not checked against `agent_definitions`. The filed item LOOKS right (row exists, type says human review, workflow reports success) and is actually in the dispatch queue: the omitted status defaulted to `'triaged'`. If the handler is also unregistered, the item detonates to `blocked` at claim (or, since commit `c8400e452` rolled, at the write door) and pins its dedup slot so later findings for the same key are silently dropped — `bugs_open/291`: tool-auditor bled 14 real findings this way over 3 days, and the wrong shape had been copied onward once already ("matches the existing pattern") before it was caught
- **the tell:** none at filing time, which is the point — `item_created` reports success either way. Later: rows at `status='blocked'`, `error='Handler agent not registered: …'`, `created_by` = your producer
- **the check:** in the step config, always set `"status"` explicitly. To park for a human: `"status": "needs_human_review"` and NO `handler_agent` (migration 217 idiom; the relaxed validation accepting that shape from config rolled with `c8400e452` — on an older binary a parked item must still name some inert handler, which is exactly how the phantom spread, so check the binary first). To dispatch: name a handler and prove it exists — `SELECT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM agent_definitions WHERE type='<handler>' AND deleted_at IS NULL);` — the docs' item-type tables are where `hitl-review` lived for four months as if real

### Firing `build-site-planner` at an ADOPTED site rewrites `pages.url`, CLEARS `pages.sections` and INSERTS canonical-name twins — and `honour_realised_identity='true'` alone did NOT stop it

- **footprint:** `agent_definitions` `type='build-site-planner'` (steps `reconcile_site_plan`, `validate_plan`, `write_site_plan`, `sync_pages` — 14 in all), `platform/orchestration/actions/write_site_plan_action.go:487`, `site_identity_policy.go` (`siteIdentityPolicyFor`, `honour_realised_identity`, `twin_identity_snap`, `stem_twin_snap`), `normaliseRealisedToPlanPage` / `parentSectionFromURL` in `v3_site_actions.go`, `datahelpers.CanonicalisePage`, `pages.url`, `pages.sections`, `site_nav_items.url`, `loancalculator_couk/canary_replan_407.sh`
- **fires when:** you replan ANY site the platform adopted rather than built — a D6-style "teach the planner what this site is" run, a `recompose_pages` release, or a canary after widening the planner's menu. The trap is about the WRITE-BACK, not the plan: a plan can be faithful and the sync still moves the site.
- **the tell: none from the run, which reports COMPLETED, and none from a page count.** Measured 2026-08-17 on `loanandmortgagecalculator.co.uk` (corr `6fe6ee93`, chassis `v1.0.1305`, 3m19s): the plan was *exactly* right in shape — 45 pages, role mix `tool 19 / guide 13 / content 9 / blog-post 2 / section-index 1 / landing 1`, identical to the live census — while the same run **INSERTED 19 twins** (`mortgages-stamp-duty` beside a new `tool-mortgages-stamp-duty` at `/tools/mortgages-stamp-duty/index.html`), **moved 21 real URLs** (`/guides/x.html` → `/guides/x/index.html`, `/loans/index.html` → `/loans.html`), **cleared `sections` to `[]` on 24 real pages**, and **repointed 2 of 5 `site_nav_items` at URLs with no deployed file**. Page count went 45 → 64, which reads like the growth an improvement loop produces.
- **the check, and do it BEFORE you fire, because afterwards a digest tells you only that *something* moved:**
  1. **Measure the fixed-point population first.** Call the real `datahelpers.CanonicalisePage` over the live page list through the descriptor `write_site_plan_action.go:487` builds — `Role`=stored `page_type`, `Slug`=`firstNonEmpty(slug,name)` (a realised page has no slug, so it is the stored NAME), `ParentSection`=`parentSectionFromURL(url)`, `FlatURLs`=`siteUsesFlatURLs`. **Never re-derive the rule in SQL** (`bugs_open/215`'s own note). Put a positive AND a negative control in the harness — a canonical page that must not move, a legacy page that must — or "nothing moved" and "the harness canonicalises nothing" print identically. On this site: **7 fixed points of 45; 38 moved; 17 by name, every one a calculator.**
  2. **Snapshot `pages` and `page_components` into bak tables**, and record `md5(name||'|'||url||'|'||page_type||'|'||status)` ordered by name. Assert the digest inside the repair transaction, not after it.
  3. **Cancel the run's `needs_rerender` item before anything claims it** — "assemble and deploy pages after plan reconcile" is what turns a DB-only mistake into a deployed one. On this run nothing had claimed it, and the live site was untouched throughout (real URLs 200, twin paths 404).
- **what SAVED this site was `rebuild_policy='owned'`, not the identity flag:** all 17 owned calculator pages came through unmodified — the run filed an `owned_page_review` item per page instead. The 24 pages it mutated were the `generic` ones. So a site whose pages are all `generic` has no such floor.
- **⚠ RESOLVED SAME DAY (2026-08-17, and the entry below is superseded by this line): the flag has an undocumented PRECONDITION — it is inert unless a SNAP or a UNION paired the page first.** `v3_site_actions.go:6476` strips `identity_authority` from every LLM page and it is *"re-stamped only by a snap or a union"*; with `twin_identity_snap` and `stem_twin_snap` absent, nothing re-stamps it, `realisedIdentityOf` returns `ok=false`, and `honour_realised_identity` is never reached. Established from the run's own `collected_data->'validate_plan'->'pages'` (realised names present, marker/url/parent_section absent, `sections: []`), `reconcile_result.pages_restamped: 0`, and the plan's URLs landing at the role's DEFAULT hub (`/tools/…`) rather than the realised parent (`/mortgages/…`) — that hub is the positive discriminator. **So seed all three switches together, and note the damage originates at the PLAN WRITE, not at `sync_pages`.**
- **⚠ superseded, kept for the shape of the mistake — the flag was ON.** `honour_realised_identity='true'` was verified live in the current structure row before the fire, and the twins were minted anyway. **Cause NOT established, deliberately** — the pairing layers `twin_identity_snap`/`stem_twin_snap` were absent on this site (the firing session's own "one canary, one question" choice, and the prime suspect: honouring a realised identity cannot help a plan page the reconciler never marked `identity_authority='realised'`), and whether the site-spec reader is in the running binary could not be settled (the sha probe of `/proc/1/exe` returned absent for its **negative control** too, so it was uninformative, not negative; the startup provenance line had scrolled). **So do not read this entry as "the flag does not work" — read it as "the flag was not sufficient on its own here, and one canary should not have been asked to answer a compound question."** 090 run correlation `33d4d7bc-62f8-4886-a8e2-7c39f0c0a302`.
- **the empty sections are a separate, older mechanism:** the plan carried 10 sections in total, all for the four pages the framework itself had built; the 41 adopted pages got none. Their slots are positional (`prose-0`, `tool-1`), which are neither a component `name` nor a `function` — `bugs_open/204`'s blindness, reaching the plan-write path on a site where 204's own fix is live. **Not `bugs_open/282`**, which is about tool-LEVEL functions missing from validate's resolver; a slot name that names nothing cannot be rescued by accepting the menu.
- **relations:** `bugs_open/215` (the twin-minting mechanism + this lane's contribution), `bugs_open/204` (positional slots), `bugs_open/241` (the URL-move hazard, measured the other way round on the sibling), `bugs_open/282`, LANDMINES "Re-adopting a site silently drops the `structure` spec's opt-in flags" (same spec row, different way to lose the same protection), `loanandmortgagecalculator_couk/NOTES_…md` entry 2026-08-17 (d) for the full account and the repair transaction
- **added:** 2026-08-17, loanandmortgagecalculator D6 planner lane

### The database is UTC and your shell is BST — so "how long has this been stuck?" done by eye is an hour wrong, and the wrong answer is a plausible incident

- **footprint:** `orchestration_states.last_activity` / `created_at` / `updated_at`, `scheduled_tasks.last_triggered_at` / `last_completed_at`, `site_work_items.updated_at`, any `::timestamp(0)` you print, and the shell's own `date`
- **fires when:** you are watching something live — a sweep, a dispatch, a scheduled task — and you compare a timestamp psql printed against the clock in your terminal to judge whether it is progressing. No symptom first: both numbers are correct, and neither is labelled.
